articles.title: Claude Code Parallel Subagent Patterns: Fan-Out, Fan-In, and Synchronization Strategies That Actually Work
articles.description: Production-tested patterns for dispatching, coordinating, and merging multiple Claude Code subagents without race conditions, context pollution, or merge overhead.
articles.body_html:
Claude Code Parallel Subagent Patterns: Fan-Out, Fan-In, and Synchronization Strategies That Actually Work

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Most parallel subagent implementations fail because teams treat them like independent workers when they are actually interdependent processes sharing a single codebase. The result is duplicate work, context pollution, and merge conflicts that consume more time than serial execution would have taken.

The pattern that teams overlook is bounded concurrency with explicit coordination. When you dispatch five subagents to analyze different parts of a monorepo, each session sees a different snapshot of the filesystem at fork time. Without synchronization barriers and merge strategies, their outputs diverge. The orchestrator ends up reconciling contradictory recommendations or silently dropping half the work.

The fix is a three-phase pattern: fan-out with bounded slots, isolated work on non-overlapping paths, and fan-in with deterministic merge order. The orchestrator enforces concurrency limits (typically three to five subagents), assigns disjoint file sets, and collects results in dependency order before applying any writes. This eliminates race conditions and makes the parallel work actually faster than serial.

This matters because parallel subagents are the only way to handle large-scale refactors or multi-package analysis within reasonable token budgets. Serial execution hits context limits around 200K tokens. Parallel patterns let you process 1M+ token codebases by partitioning the work, but only if you control the coordination overhead.

Key Takeaways

  • Unbounded parallel subagents produce context pollution and merge conflicts that erase any speed gains.
  • The production sweet spot is three to five concurrent subagents working on disjoint file sets with explicit merge order.
  • Fan-out requires slot limits and path isolation; fan-in requires dependency-aware result collection before applying writes.
  • Synchronization barriers at phase boundaries prevent race conditions without blocking parallelism during independent work.
  • Real-world parallel patterns save 60-70% wall time on monorepo analysis, but only when merge overhead stays under 15% of total execution.

Fan-Out Pattern: Dispatching Multiple Subagents Simultaneously

The fan-out pattern dispatches multiple subagents at once, each handling a discrete slice of the overall task. The failure mode here is subtle but expensive: launching ten subagents to "analyze the codebase" without explicit boundaries creates ten overlapping contexts. Each session reads shared files, proposes conflicting changes, and the orchestrator spends more time reconciling than you saved by parallelizing.

The correct pattern enforces three constraints before dispatch. First, the orchestrator calculates a bounded concurrency limit based on token budget and task complexity. Three to five slots is the tested range for most monorepo work. Second, the orchestrator partitions the input space into disjoint sets: packages, modules, feature directories, or test suites. Third, each subagent receives an explicit scope that prevents overlap. The orchestrator holds a queue of pending tasks and releases new work only when a slot opens.

This structure prevents context pollution because no two subagents read or write overlapping files. When Subagent A works on src/auth and Subagent B works on src/api, their file reads are isolated. The orchestrator tracks which paths are in-flight and holds back tasks that would violate the disjoint guarantee until conflicting work completes.

The token budget constraint matters because each subagent session carries its own context window. If you dispatch ten subagents simultaneously on a 200K token codebase, you burn 2M tokens in parallel. The API rate limits and cost controls both fail. Bounded slots keep total active context predictable: five subagents at 40K tokens each is 200K simultaneous usage, which fits within most team quotas.

Parallel subagent orchestration dashboard

The orchestrator implementation uses a simple state machine. The queue is a priority list of pending scopes. The active set tracks running subagent sessions. When a subagent completes, the orchestrator marks that slot available and pulls the next task from the queue. The transition logic ensures you never exceed your slot limit and never double-book a file path.

Fan-In Pattern: Collecting and Merging Subagent Results

Fan-in is where most parallel implementations break. The orchestrator receives five result sets from completed subagents and needs to produce a single coherent output. The naive approach concatenates all results and hands them to a final merge session. This fails because merge complexity grows quadratically with the number of inputs. Five 10K token reports become a 50K token merge task that the final session cannot process without losing context on half the recommendations.

The working pattern is dependency-ordered collection with incremental merge. The orchestrator maintains a dependency graph of the original scopes. When src/ui depends on types from src/api, the orchestrator collects the src/api results first, applies those changes to the working tree, and then merges src/ui results against the updated state. This converts an N-way merge into N sequential 2-way merges, each of which fits comfortably in context.

interface SubagentResult {
  scope: string;
  changes: FileChange[];
  summary: string;
  dependencies: string[];
}

async function fanInResults(
  results: SubagentResult[],
  depGraph: DependencyGraph
): Promise<MergedOutput> {
  const sorted = topologicalSort(results, depGraph);
  let workingTree = await loadBaseTree();
  const mergedChanges: FileChange[] = [];

  for (const result of sorted) {
    // Apply changes to working tree in dependency order
    const resolved = await resolveConflicts(
      result.changes,
      workingTree
    );
    workingTree = await applyChanges(workingTree, resolved);
    mergedChanges.push(...resolved);
  }

  return {
    changes: mergedChanges,
    tree: workingTree,
    summary: await generateSummary(mergedChanges)
  };
}

The resolveConflicts function is the critical piece. When Subagent A and Subagent B both modify the same import statement, the resolver uses the dependency order to pick a winner. If A ran first in topological order, its change stands and B's overlapping edit is dropped. The alternative is a merge session that reads both proposals and synthesizes a solution, but that consumes tokens and adds latency. Dependency order gives you a deterministic resolution policy for free.

The summary generation step happens after all changes are applied. This ensures the final summary reflects the actual merged state, not the sum of individual subagent summaries. Each subagent summary described what it changed in isolation. The orchestrator summary describes what changed in the final codebase after all merges, which is what the reader needs to review.

In other words, fan-in is not a concatenation operation. Fan-in is a graph traversal that applies changes in topological order and generates a single authoritative summary at the end. The difference between these two approaches is the difference between a working parallel system and one that produces garbage.

Synchronization Strategies: Coordinating Parallel Work Without Race Conditions

Synchronization barriers prevent race conditions during parallel execution. The failure mode teams hit is concurrent writes to shared state: two subagents both update package.json dependencies, and the second write silently clobbers the first. The orchestrator has no visibility into which version won, and the final state is nondeterministic.

The working pattern uses phase-based execution with explicit barriers. Phase one is read-only analysis. All subagents execute in parallel, reading files and generating recommendations without writing anything. The orchestrator blocks phase two until all phase one work completes. Phase two is write execution. The orchestrator applies changes from phase one in dependency order, with no new reads allowed. This eliminates read-write and write-write hazards because reads and writes never overlap.

The barrier implementation is a semaphore that counts completed subagents. When the count reaches the total number of dispatched sessions, the orchestrator releases the next phase. Between phases, the orchestrator can inject validation steps: running tests, checking type correctness, or verifying that no uncommitted changes exist before proceeding.

Lock-based coordination is an alternative pattern for fine-grained synchronization. The orchestrator maintains a lock table keyed by file path. Before a subagent reads or writes a file, it acquires a read lock or write lock. Read locks are shared, write locks are exclusive. This allows concurrent reads of the same file while serializing writes. The downside is lock contention overhead: if five subagents all need to read tsconfig.json, they all succeed, but if they all need to write it, four of them block.

The production tradeoff is phase-based barriers for coarse-grained tasks (analyzing separate packages) and lock-based coordination for fine-grained tasks (updating shared configuration files). The key is making the synchronization policy explicit in the orchestrator code. Implicit coordination through "hoping subagents do not collide" is how you get nondeterministic failures in production.

The verification phase at the end catches synchronization bugs that slipped through. After all writes complete, a final subagent runs type checking, linting, and tests against the merged result. If verification fails, the orchestrator can roll back to the pre-write state and retry with stricter barriers. This makes synchronization failures visible instead of silent.

Real-World Example: Parallel Codebase Analysis with Bounded Concurrency

A practical use case is analyzing a TypeScript monorepo to find unused exports across 50 packages. Serial execution would load all 50 packages into a single context and run out of tokens around package 30. Parallel execution partitions the packages into five groups of ten and runs five concurrent subagents.

interface AnalysisTask {
  packages: string[];
  maxTokens: number;
}

async function parallelUnusedExportAnalysis(
  monorepoRoot: string,
  concurrency: number = 5
): Promise<UnusedExportReport> {
  const packages = await discoverPackages(monorepoRoot);
  const tasks = partitionPackages(packages, concurrency);

  const results = await Promise.all(
    tasks.map(task => 
      analyzePackageGroup(task, monorepoRoot)
    )
  );

  return mergeAnalysisResults(results);
}

async function analyzePackageGroup(
  task: AnalysisTask,
  root: string
): Promise<PartialReport> {
  const subagent = await spawnSubagent({
    workingDir: root,
    scope: task.packages,
    maxTokens: task.maxTokens
  });

  const exports = await subagent.findExports(task.packages);
  const imports = await subagent.findImports(task.packages);

  return {
    unused: exports.filter(exp => 
      !imports.some(imp => imp.references(exp))
    ),
    scope: task.packages
  };
}

The partitionPackages function uses package dependency graphs to create disjoint groups. Packages that import from each other stay in the same group to avoid cross-group reference checking. Independent packages split across groups for maximum parallelism. This partitioning strategy keeps each subagent task self-contained while maintaining correctness.

The merge step combines the partial reports into a single unused export list. Because each group was disjoint, there are no duplicate entries to reconcile. The orchestrator sorts the final list by package name and generates a summary showing which packages have the most dead code. The total wall time is one-fifth of serial execution because five subagents run simultaneously, and merge overhead is negligible because the partial results do not overlap.

Monorepo analysis performance comparison

The token budget for this pattern is predictable. Each subagent processes ten packages at roughly 8K tokens per package, so 80K tokens per session. Five sessions in parallel is 400K total tokens in-flight. The orchestrator itself uses minimal tokens to coordinate, so the total cost stays under 450K tokens for a 50-package monorepo. Serial execution would hit 500K+ tokens and fail before completion.

This pattern extends to other codebase-wide analyses: dead code elimination, dependency audits, type coverage reports, or test file generation. The key is partitioning the input space so each subagent works on a disjoint subset and the merge operation is cheap. When merge complexity starts to dominate, you have partitioned too finely and need to reduce concurrency or increase partition size.

Common Pitfalls: Duplicate Execution, Context Pollution, and Merge Overhead

The first pitfall is duplicate execution from overlapping scopes. When the orchestrator assigns src/api to Subagent A and src/ to Subagent B, both sessions analyze src/api. The orchestrator receives two reports on the same files and wastes tokens on redundant work. The fix is strict disjoint partitioning at dispatch time. If a scope overlaps with an in-flight task, the orchestrator holds it in the queue until the conflicting task completes.

Context pollution happens when subagents share mutable state. If two subagents both read a shared cache file, update it with their findings, and write it back, the last write wins and earlier results disappear. The fix is copy-on-write caches or read-only shared state with write-once outputs. Each subagent gets a private workspace for intermediate results and only the orchestrator writes to shared storage after merging.

Merge overhead kills performance when the number of subagents exceeds the natural partition count. Analyzing a monorepo with six packages using ten subagents means four subagents handle one package each and six handle one package each. The orchestrator now merges ten result sets instead of six, and the extra four provide no parallelism benefit. The fix is matching concurrency to the partition count. If you have six natural partitions, run six subagents, not ten.

The threshold where merge overhead dominates is around 15% of total execution time. If you spend 85 seconds on parallel analysis and 15 seconds merging results, you are at the limit. Increasing concurrency beyond that point increases merge time faster than it decreases analysis time. The 3-5 subagent rule comes from empirical observation that most codebases have 3-5 natural partitions (frontend, backend, shared libraries, tests, configuration) and pushing beyond that hits diminishing returns.

The implication here is that parallel patterns are not universally better than serial. They win when the input space has natural disjoint partitions, the merge operation is cheap relative to the work, and the concurrency limit fits the partition count. Forcing parallelism onto inherently sequential tasks (like applying a series of dependent type migrations) adds coordination overhead without speed gains.

Production Patterns: The 3-5 Subagent Rule and When to Break It

The 3-5 concurrent subagent limit is the tested production default for monorepo analysis, multi-package refactors, and codebase-wide search tasks. This range balances parallelism gains against merge overhead and token budget constraints. Three subagents is the minimum to see meaningful speedup. Five subagents is the maximum before merge complexity starts to eat the gains.

Breaking this rule makes sense in two scenarios. First, when the task is embarrassingly parallel with no merge step. Generating documentation for 20 independent packages can run 20 subagents because each output is a standalone file with no cross-references. The orchestrator collects 20 markdown files and writes them to disk without any merge logic.

Second, when token budget allows higher concurrency without hitting rate limits. If your team quota is 2M tokens per minute and each subagent uses 50K tokens, you can run 40 concurrent sessions before hitting the limit. The constraint shifts from token budget to orchestrator complexity. Managing 40 in-flight sessions requires robust error handling, retry logic, and progress tracking that a 5-session orchestrator does not need.

The production pattern for high-concurrency scenarios is hierarchical orchestration. A top-level orchestrator spawns five mid-level orchestrators, each managing five subagents. This keeps each orchestrator's active set manageable while achieving 25-way parallelism. The mid-level orchestrators handle local fan-in and report summaries to the top level, which does the final merge. This pattern scales to hundreds of tasks without overwhelming a single orchestrator session.

The breaking point for this pattern is when coordination overhead exceeds work time. If your orchestrator spends 60% of wall time scheduling tasks and 40% waiting for subagents, you have over-parallelized. The fix is reducing concurrency or increasing task granularity so each subagent does more work per dispatch. The goal is keeping orchestrator idle time (waiting for subagents) above 70% of total time. That indicates the parallelism is doing useful work.

A practical heuristic for setting concurrency is task count divided by four, capped at five. Ten tasks run on three subagents (10 / 4 = 2.5, round up to 3). Twenty tasks run on five subagents (20 / 4 = 5, which hits the cap). Forty tasks run on five subagents with hierarchical orchestration (top-level cap), not ten subagents (which would exceed the merge overhead threshold). This heuristic keeps merge complexity linear and orchestrator logic simple.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do you prevent two subagents from modifying the same file?

The orchestrator assigns disjoint file scopes before dispatch and tracks which paths are in-flight. If a new task would overlap an active scope, the orchestrator queues it until the conflicting task completes. During the write phase, changes are applied sequentially in dependency order so only one session touches each file.

What happens when a subagent crashes mid-execution?

The orchestrator detects the failure through promise rejection or timeout and marks that scope as available for retry. The failed task goes back into the queue with incremented retry count. After three failures, the orchestrator logs the error and continues with remaining tasks so one broken scope does not block the entire workflow.

Can subagents communicate with each other during execution?

No, subagents are isolated sessions with no direct communication channel. All coordination happens through the orchestrator. If Subagent A needs data from Subagent B, the orchestrator collects B's result first and passes it to A as input. This enforces dependency order and prevents race conditions.

How do you verify that parallel execution produced the same result as serial?

Run a final verification subagent after all merges complete. This session type-checks the merged code, runs tests, and compares the output against known-good baselines. If verification fails, the orchestrator can roll back changes and retry with serial execution as a fallback to identify which parallel merge introduced the error.

When should you use serial execution instead of parallel?

Use serial when tasks have strict sequential dependencies (migration step B requires completed migration step A), when the codebase is small enough to fit in a single context (under 100K tokens), or when merge complexity would exceed 15% of total execution time (typically when you would need more than five subagents but natural partitions are fewer than three).

Conclusion: Building Your Parallel Subagent Playbook

The essential patterns for production parallel subagents are bounded concurrency with disjoint scopes, phase-based synchronization barriers, and dependency-ordered fan-in. These three pieces eliminate the race conditions, context pollution, and merge overhead that break naive parallel implementations.

Start with the 3-5 subagent rule for monorepo analysis and multi-package refactors. Partition your input space into natural boundaries like package roots or feature directories. Enforce read-only analysis phases followed by sequential write phases. Merge results in topological dependency order, not chronological completion order.

Break the concurrency limit only for embarrassingly parallel tasks with no merge step or when you implement hierarchical orchestration for hundreds of tasks. Monitor merge overhead and pull back when it exceeds 15% of wall time. The goal is keeping orchestrator idle time above 70%, which indicates parallelism is doing real work instead of just adding coordination complexity.

That covers the essential patterns for parallel Claude Code subagents. Apply these in production and the difference will be immediate. Your monorepo analysis tasks will run in one-fifth the wall time, your token budgets will stay predictable, and your merge conflicts will disappear because disjoint scopes prevent them from happening in the first place.

articles.body_html:
o1's API dies on Oct 23 — six days from now. Not deprecated-with-a-warning. Shutdown: calls to the model ID fail, no grace traffic, no automatic remap.

And it's not just o1. Three cliffs, all sourced from valueaddvc's "OpenAI API Pricing 2026" (Oct 15 2026), citing OpenAI's deprecations page:

  • Oct 23, 2026 — o1, o1-pro, o3-mini, o4-mini
  • Dec 11, 2026 — o3, o3-pro, gpt-5 family
  • Jan 14, 2027 — gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini

The failure mode is always the same: a model ID hardcoded somewhere — app code, a worker config, a fallback chain — and nobody finds it until the API starts 404ing.

The scanner

The naive approach is grep -r "o1". The problem with naive grep:

  • gpt-4o matches inside gpt-4o-mini (double report)
  • o1 matches inside o1-pro (split token)
  • gpt-5.6 must never read as gpt-5

The fix is one compiled regex: alternation ordered longest-first, strict token boundaries, plus a dot-digit guard:

import re

MODEL_RE = re.compile(
    r"(?<![\w])(?:gpt-4o-mini|gpt-5-[\w.-]+|gpt-4o|o1-pro|o3-pro|o3-mini|o4-mini|gpt-5|o1|o3)(?![\w-])(?!\.\d)",
    re.IGNORECASE,
)
  • (?<![\w]) / (?![\w-]) — the match must start/end on a token boundary, so o1 never fires inside o1-pro (longest-first ordering handles that too) and gpt-4o never fires inside gpt-4o-mini.
  • (?!\.\d) — the dot-digit guard: gpt-5.6 must never read as gpt-5.
  • re.IGNORECASE — because O1-PRO in a config file is the same cliff.

Then map each hit to its cliff:

# Shutdown cliffs. Dates: valueaddvc.com "OpenAI API Pricing 2026" (Oct 15 2026),
# citing OpenAI's deprecations page. None = no OpenAI-named target: you pick, then verify.
CLIFFS = {
    "o1": ("2026-10-23", "GPT-5.6 Sol"),
    "o1-pro": ("2026-10-23", "GPT-5.6 Sol"),
    "o3-mini": ("2026-10-23", "GPT-5.6 Sol"),
    "o4-mini": ("2026-10-23", "GPT-5.6 Terra"),
    "o3": ("2026-12-11", "GPT-5.6 Sol"),
    "o3-pro": ("2026-12-11", "GPT-5.6 Sol"),
    "gpt-5": ("2026-12-11", None),
    "gpt-4o": ("2027-01-14", "GPT-6 Luna"),
    "gpt-4o-mini": ("2027-01-14", None),
}

def canonical(hit: str) -> str:
    h = hit.lower()
    return "gpt-5" if h.startswith("gpt-5-") else h

def scan(text: str):
    """One hit per dying model ID: shutdown date + OpenAI-named replacement."""
    hits, seen = [], set()
    for m in MODEL_RE.finditer(text):
        if m.start() in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(m.start())
        key = canonical(m.group(0))
        shutdown, replacement = CLIFFS[key]
        hits.append({
            "match": m.group(0),
            "model": key,
            "shutdown": shutdown,
            "replacement": replacement,
        })
    return hits

Edge cases, tested:

  • gpt-4o-mini → one hit (gpt-4o-mini, Jan 14). Never double-reports as gpt-4o.
  • O1-PRO → one hit (o1-pro, Oct 23). Case-insensitive.
  • gpt-5.6 Sol → zero hits. The dot-digit guard holds.

And a thin API wrapper if you want it behind HTTP:

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()

class ScanRequest(BaseModel):
    text: str

@app.post("/scan")
def scan_endpoint(req: ScanRequest):
    return {"hits": scan(req.text)}

POST a codebase or config dump, get per-hit shutdown dates and the OpenAI-named replacement.

The replacement math

OpenAI named the replacements itself:

  • o1 / o3-mini / o3 (+ pro variants) → GPT-5.6 Sol
  • o4-mini → GPT-5.6 Terra
  • gpt-4o → GPT-6 Luna at $0.10/$0.50 per 1M
  • gpt-5 snapshots and gpt-4o-mini got no named target — you pick, then verify.

Worked at 10M input / 10M output tokens per month (rates: valueaddvc, Oct 15 2026):

  • o1 → Sol: $750 → $240 (−$510/mo)
  • gpt-4o → Luna: $125 → $6

o3 → Sol looks like $100 → $240 on sticker — up — but the hidden-thinking line item disappears, so the real bill usually drops hard.

The bill-killer nobody budgets: hidden reasoning tokens. o1/o3 burn 5K–20K per answer — invisible, billed at output rate. o3 can cost 10–15x GPT-4o for the same question once hidden reasoning tokens hit the bill.

One more trap: GPT-5.6 Sol is on promo — $4/$20 per 1M through Nov 21, 2026, then list $5/$30. Budget the migration at list. The promo is a gift, not a plan.

Verification checklist

  • Confirm every rate and date against OpenAI's live pricing and deprecations pages. The kit is an Oct 15 snapshot, not a live feed.
  • Budget Sol at list ($5/$30), not promo ($4/$20 through Nov 21, 2026).
  • Diarize the promo cliffs too: Nov 21 (Sol), Dec 1 (Gemini 4 Argon $2/$10 → $4/$20), Jan 1 (Gemini 3.8 Flash $0.75/$3.75 → $1.50/$7.50).
  • Eval the replacement on staging before prod — reasoning models aren't drop-in.
  • Set a spend guard post-migration: O(1) budget check, hard 402 cutoff, kill switch, fail closed on unpriced models.

Disclaimer: dates/rates from valueaddvc.com "OpenAI API Pricing 2026" (Oct 15 2026), citing OpenAI docs. It's a snapshot, not a live feed — verify against OpenAI's live pricing page before migrating. Evidence kit, not financial advice.

The full kit — scanner, replacement map, 72-hour Oct-23 checklist, spend-guard pattern — is $29 one-time: https://vittoriali.gumroad.com/l/cutoff

articles.body_html:
Yooooooo... wassup developers!! How are you all?? 😭

So, still no new users... which means old stats = new stats 😂

Today is Day 16 of building my project, a social media platform named Crowdwide, standing at 11 users and 40+ posts.

So, I feel like there is no need to add new features just to maintain the flow. Now, I need to focus on getting users onto the platform!

To make login and signup easier for users, I added the GitHub login/create account option to Crowdwide.

And nothing much new is there...

Also, I got 12+ emails from other companies and 4+ from YouTubers for promoting Crowdwide. I accepted only 2 out of all of them.

I mean, I'm building everything with a 0 budget. That's why 😭 I'm 15, and I can't make payments.

And out of those two, one is building a startup/website platform, and he agreed to a partnership with Crowdwide!

That's the first time I've ever gotten a partnership with any platform or website owner. 🥹

I also applied to some platforms to get a parent-child monetization system for Crowdwide.

Like:

Crowdwide platform → Communities under Crowdwide get monetized → Community owners earn money.

But the platforms providing this require a large amount of traffic and so many other things...

The thing I need most at this moment is USERS! 😭

Also, from the stats, I got to know that Sunday is when most Crowdwide users revisit the platform!!

YEAAAAAAAA!! 🔥

According to the stats, I think most of them are coming from the newsletter, but they still come back, like a few posts, make some comments, and engage!

I've noticed that Saturday and Sunday are the best days for promoting posts, articles, polls, and communities.

It works well!

BTW, if you have any ideas or thoughts, you can share them! I'll definitely discuss them.

Crowdwide: https://www.crowdwide.run.place/

Open source: https://github.com/DeveloperPuneet/Crowdwide

articles.body_html:
If you’ve ever had to integrate ZKTeco biometric time-and-attendance clocks (fingerprint scanners, facial recognition terminals, RFID readers) into a modern web stack, you already know the grim reality of the ecosystem:

  • Most existing Packagist packages are 6 to 10 years old abandonware.
  • They throw fatal deprecation notices on PHP 8.1, 8.2, 8.3, and 8.4.
  • They are strictly UDP-only—meaning when deployed across remote offices over WAN routers or NAT firewalls, UDP packets drop silently without error messages.
  • None of them support writing attendance back to the machine. If an employee forgot to clock in or your web app needs to push an authorized remote punch, you were told "it's impossible without ZKTeco's proprietary Windows C++ DLLs".

I decided to fix this once and for all. I reverse-engineered the binary protocol and built taha-rafi/php-zkteco (v2.1.0).

1. The Protocol Problem: UDP vs. TCP in Enterprise Networks

The original ZK protocol was designed in the late 1990s around raw UDP datagrams (CMD_CONNECT: 1000). While UDP is fast on a local switch, modern distributed enterprises connect clocks across branch offices, cloud VPNs, and port-forwarded WAN routers.

In php-zkteco, we implemented a Dual-Protocol Engine with automatic fallback:

use TahaRafi\ZKTeco\ZKTeco;
use TahaRafi\ZKTeco\Constants;

// Automatically tries TCP stream first, then transparently falls back to UDP
$zk = new ZKTeco('192.168.1.201', 4370, commKey: 0, protocol: Constants::PROTOCOL_AUTO);

if ($zk->connectWithRetry(maxRetries: 3, retryDelayMs: 400)) {
    echo "Connected via: " . $zk->getActiveProtocol(); // TCP or UDP
}

The TCP implementation encapsulates packets with a 32-bit length header (0x5050827D) and handles keep-alive pinging, ensuring zero packet drops across WAN routers.

2. Reverse-Engineering Direct Hardware Attendance Writing (CMD_SET_DATA 3001)

Reading logs from a biometric clock is easy (CMD_ATTLOG_RRQ: 501). But what happens when an HR manager manually approves a punch in your Laravel app and you need the physical biometric terminal to recognize it?

Through packet analysis of ZKTeco's internal protocol, we uncovered the payload schema required to write directly to the machine's internal Flash table (ATT_LOG):

TableName=ATT_LOG\r\nUser_PIN={UID}\tVerify_Type={VT}\tVerify_Time={TIMESTAMP}\tStatus={STATE}\tWork_Code_ID=0\0

By packaging this buffer with CMD_SET_DATA (3001) and immediately dispatching CMD_REFRESHDATA (1013) with CMD_VOICE (1014), the machine not only permanently logs the check-in/out record inside its memory—it also plays the hardware voice: "Thank you"!

// Write a punch directly to physical hardware memory:
$zk->markAttendance(
    userId: '101',
    state: Constants::ATT_STATE_CHECK_IN,
    timestamp: '2026-10-17 09:00:00',
    verifyType: Constants::VERIFY_FINGERPRINT,
    options: [
        'write_to_device' => true,
        'device_feedback' => true // Triggers machine voice & LCD display
    ]
);

3. Laravel 8–12 Native Support (Zero Configuration)

We included an automatic ServiceProvider and Facade. In any Laravel project:

composer require taha-rafi/php-zkteco

articles.title: Your Public Beta Needs a Bug Report a Stranger Can Reproduce
articles.description: Give public beta testers a short way to report what they tried, what they expected, and what...
articles.body_html:
Give public beta testers a short way to report what they tried, what they expected, and what happened. Then turn that report into a separate developer reproduction note with a known starting state, exact steps and the environment you checked. Don't make the tester do your whole debugging job.

Building in public can bring people to an unfinished product. It also creates a handoff problem: a useful comment such as “the import stopped” is not yet enough for somebody else to repeat the failure. Treat the comment as the beginning of a report, rather than proof that the reporter did something wrong.

The workflow below uses two linked records. One captures the tester's observation with little effort. The other records the developer's investigation. Keeping those jobs separate helps you preserve what was actually reported while adding the detail needed to act.

Ask for the smallest useful first report

Start with the task, the action that failed, the visible result and the expected result. Give the tester a clear route to send those details, including a private route when the information should not be public.

Ask for environment details the person can reasonably provide. “Which browser and device were you using?” is accessible. “Attach a sanitized request trace” may be too much for somebody who volunteered to try an invoice tool.

Make screenshots optional when a plain description will do. A screen can contain client names, file paths, email addresses or other information that does not belong in a public discussion. Explain what to leave out before asking for an attachment.

Don't collect every possible field just because your tracker supports it. If a version is already clear from the beta link, you can add it yourself. The first report needs enough information for the next question, not a complete diagnostic archive.

Keep the reporter's observation separate from your diagnosis

Write down what the tester saw before adding a theory about why it happened. “The spinner stayed visible after selecting Import” is an observation. “The server timed out” is a diagnosis that needs evidence.

If the reporter supplies a theory, preserve it as their suggestion. Do not silently turn it into the ticket's confirmed cause. A useful investigation can begin with an incomplete description without making the description more certain than it is.

Ask a narrow follow-up when needed. You might need to know whether the person started from a new project or reopened an existing one. That distinction is easier to answer than a general request for more information.

Keep the original report linked to your investigation note. When you later reproduce a similar symptom under different conditions, you will need to check whether you found the same problem or a different one.

Use a report format people can understand

GitHub's issue-form documentation shows examples that collect current behavior, expected behavior, reproduction steps and environment. It also supports different field types and validation. Those are tools for structuring a report, not a reason to require every field from every tester.

For a small public beta, a plain form or message can ask: what were you trying to do, where did you begin, which action changed the screen, what appeared, and what did you expect instead?

Let the person say that they do not know an answer. A guessed software version is less useful than an unknown one. You can often narrow the environment later without asking them to become familiar with your release process.

If you use a public issue tracker, say that before submission. A tester should not discover that their attachment is public only after sending it. Keep account-specific investigation in an appropriate private support route.

Build a developer note from a known starting state

Once you have the initial report, write the state needed to repeat the attempt. Include the relevant build, browser, account role and sample data. Add only details that help distinguish this attempt from a different one.

The starting state can matter as much as the clicks. An empty workspace, an existing import mapping and a previously failed upload are different conditions. If you reset the product before testing, record that reset.

Use one action per step and name the visible control. “Open a new workspace, select the sample file, then press Import” is easier to inspect than “try uploading as usual.” State the result at the step where the behavior diverges.

Keep an exact error message when it is safe to do so. Preserve relevant punctuation and wording. Remove secrets and private identifiers rather than pasting an entire log into a public ticket.

Work through a fictional CSV import failure

Imagine a fictional beta product that imports a list of workshop registrations. A tester says that importing a file stops at the mapping screen. They expected to see a confirmation showing the imported rows. This is an invented example, not a report from a real beta.

The developer asks whether the file has a header row and whether a mapping was already saved. The tester says it has a header and that they reused yesterday's workspace. The developer now has two conditions worth checking without assuming either one is the cause.

The first reproduction note uses a fresh workspace and a small invented file with name and session columns. The import succeeds. Record that result as a successful attempt under those conditions, rather than closing the original report as user error.

The next attempt starts with a saved mapping, then imports a file with one column renamed. If the failure appears there, record the exact sequence and the visible difference. You have narrowed a condition; you have not yet proved the underlying cause.

Say unreproduced when you have not reproduced it

An unreproduced report is a legitimate state. It means the investigation has not repeated the reported behavior under the conditions checked. It does not mean the person imagined it or that the product is reliable in every environment.

List the attempts that matter and the next missing detail. In the fictional example, you might still need to learn whether the original file contained an empty column. That is a concrete question the tester can answer without providing private registration data.

Avoid a long sequence of speculative requests. Each new question should help distinguish plausible conditions. If the reporter is no longer available, preserve the gap and decide what you can check independently.

When a workaround exists, describe the conditions you actually verified. “Creating a new mapping worked with our sample file” is more accurate than “just reset everything.” Be clear if the workaround would remove saved work or impose another cost.

Return a useful status to the public thread

If the report began under a public beta invitation, return with a short status that does not expose the private investigation. Say whether the issue is reproduced, still being checked, or fixed in a named available build.

Do not publish a cheerful fixed message when the change is only in a local branch. Describe the state precisely. A fix that exists but is not available to testers has not yet repaired their experience.

Invite a recheck only when the relevant version is available and participation remains optional. Give the original steps and explain which behavior should now differ. The tester should not have to rediscover the entire report to help again.

Buildside is a place for founders to share progress and questions. I founded it. A public update can explain the investigation and its limits, while the detailed report stays in the place suited to its data.

Measure the quality of the handoff

The useful question is whether another developer can reach the relevant state and inspect the claimed failure. Counted fields and long attachments cannot answer that on their own.

Before closing the ticket, ask somebody to follow the reproduction note without your verbal explanation if you have that help available. For a solo project, return to the note after a break and check which steps depended on memory.

Record what remains untested after a fix. One repaired sequence does not establish that every import combination works. Keep the scope of the public claim close to the scope of the check.

Before your next public beta invitation, try your own reporting route. Make a small invented report, turn it into a reproduction note, and identify the point where a stranger would need to ask what you meant.

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

Beat Online Discounts & Keep Your Walk-in Customers

A 100% client-side, zero-server competitive pricing intelligence assistant designed specifically for brick-and-mortar retail shop owners.

What I Built

The Problem: Showrooming & Predatory E-Commerce Discounts

Every single day, independent offline store owners (clothing boutiques, electronics & mobile stores, kirana supermarkets, and footwear outlets) face the exact same frustrating scenario:
A customer walks into the physical store, tries on a jacket, inspects a phone, or asks about groceries, pulls out their smartphone, and says:

"I saw this ₹500 cheaper online on Amazon / Flipkart! Can you match the price?"

Most offline shopkeepers panic: they either give in and slash their hard-earned profit margins, or refuse and watch the customer walk straight out the door.

The Solution: PricePulse AI

PricePulse AI is a zero-server, privacy-first competitive intelligence dashboard running 100% inside the shopkeeper's web browser. In under 2 seconds, the store owner can paste any online product link and enter their current shop price.

PricePulse immediately analyzes the competitor listing and equips the shopkeeper with an In-Store Action Plan:

  1. 🎯 Risk to Shop (The Pulse Meter): An animated SVG gauge calculating an instant threat score (0–100) that categorizes whether the competitor move is a negligible online illusion or an aggressive flash sale requiring defensive action.
  2. 📊 Your Shop vs. Competitor (The Diff Matrix): A 4-card transition grid showing where physical retail beats e-commerce:
    • Price Comparison: True delta percentage between in-store price and online listed price.
    • Delivery vs. Instant Take-Home: Comparing courier delays (3–6 days) and hidden handling fees vs. immediate take-home tonight.
    • In-Store Trial & Perks: Hands-on trial room fitting, audio testing, and personal service vs. online return friction.
    • Trust & Warranty: Instant 1-to-1 in-store counter replacement vs. courier return hassles and lost parcels.
  3. 🗣️ Staff Counter-Script (Objection Handler): Word-for-word spoken dialogue for sales assistants to counter "I saw it cheaper online" objections confidently on the spot.
  4. 💬 WhatsApp Customer Broadcast: Engaging, high-converting messages with emojis tailored for the store's VIP broadcast list or WhatsApp Status.
  5. 📋 Shop Counter Signboard: High-impact text ready to print on an A4 sheet for checkout counters, fitting rooms, or chalkboard easels.
  6. 🎁 In-Store Margin Bundle & Playbook: Smart accessory add-ons and value shields that close walk-ins without sacrificing product margins.

Who Would Pay For It?

  • Independent Retail Store Owners: Boutique clothing shops, mobile/laptop retail stores, consumer electronics dealers, optical stores, and neighborhood kiranas.
  • Retail Store Managers & Franchises: Multi-branch retailers needing standardized staff counter-scripts so sales staff don't give unauthorized cash discounts.
  • Commercial Viability: As a $12/month or $99/year micro-SaaS, or bundled as a one-time digital kit for local retail associations. Because it runs 100% client-side, the operational hosting cost is $0.00, making gross margins near 100%.

Demo

  • Live Web App: https://ujjwalgupta2021.github.io/PricePulse-AI/ (Deployable to GitHub Pages with 0 server configuration)
  • Built-in Interactive Demos (Zero Setup Required): Clicking any demo button instantly simulates real retail defense scenarios without requiring an API key:
    • 👕 Clothing Boutique: Arctic Expedition Parka vs. discount e-commerce apparel seller.
    • 📱 Mobile & Electronics: Noise-Cancelling Wireless Headphones vs. online tech marketplace.
    • 🛒 Supermarket / Kirana: Premium Basmati Rice & Oil Combo vs. quick-commerce delivery apps.
  • Theme Switcher: Full support for both Dark Glassmorphic Theme and clean, high-contrast Light Retail Theme.

Code

  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/ujjwalgupta2021/PricePulse-AI
  • Core Architecture:
    • index.html — Clean semantic structure, SVG gauge meters, and accessibility-first modal views.
    • styles.css — Modern glassmorphism system with CSS custom properties, responsive grids, and dark/light modes.
    • js/app.js — Application lifecycle, event orchestration, and markdown export engine.
    • js/gemini.js — Direct HTTPS connection to Google Gemini Flash with automatic model negotiation and resilient JSON parsing.
    • js/scraper.js — Client-side scraping bridge cascading across Jina Reader AI, AllOrigins, and URL slug anti-bot extractors.
    • js/pulse-meter.js — High-performance SVG needle rotation and stroke-dashoffset animation.
    • js/diff-matrix.js — High-contrast side-by-side transition cards comparing baseline vs. live page data.
    • js/counter-attack.js — Multi-tab action plan generator with 1-click clipboard copy.
    • js/storage.js — 100% client-side LocalStorage vault for private keys, preferences, and watchlist.

How I Built It

1. Pure Open-Innovation & Client-Side Agent Harness

PricePulse AI was built without any backend servers, Python microservices, or node daemons. The entire application runs directly inside the client's browser as a zero-server agent harness:

  • Vanilla HTML5 & CSS3: No bloated CSS frameworks or heavyweight JavaScript bundles; initial load takes < 150ms.
  • Client-Side Scraping Bridge: Directly reads competitor product listings using Jina Reader AI (https://r.jina.ai/), AllOrigins proxy, and an intelligent URL slug parser with Amazon/Flipkart anti-bot detection.
  • Open-Weight & Model-Agnostic Architecture: Built around the open HTTP standard for generative inference. While it pairs natively with Google Gemini Flash for speed (<600ms), its modular schema engine is compatible with open-weight models (including Google Gemma 2B/9B, Llama 3, and Mistral via local WebLLM or Ollama proxies).

2. Google Gemini Flash Integration with Dynamic Model Auto-Negotiation

PricePulse connects directly to Google AI Studio's Gemini Flash REST API (generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta):

  • Automated Catalog Discovery: The engine queries ModelService.ListModels to dynamically discover supported models on the user's key (gemini-1.5-flash, gemini-2.0-flash, gemini-3.8-flash) without requiring confusing manual dropdown configuration.
  • Strict Schema Steering: Uses official system instructions with JSON response constraints to ensure high-fidelity retail defense outputs.
  • Resilient JSON Parser: Employs regex { ... } substring recovery to gracefully extract valid data even if the model outputs conversational text.
  • Fail-Safe Retail Intelligence Shield: If the AI API experiences network disconnects or quota rate limits, PricePulse automatically activates an offline synthesized retail audit using the real URL, extracted product title, and store baseline, ensuring 0% crash rate.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  1. Zero Recurring Overhead for Mom-and-Pop Retailers:

    Most commercial retail software costs $50–$200/month because of cloud servers, databases, and middleman APIs. By utilizing open web standards, free-tier client-side AI, and static hosting, offline store owners can access enterprise-grade competitive intelligence without paying hefty SaaS subscriptions.

  2. Absolute Privacy of Store Margins & Wholesale Pricing:

    Local shopkeepers will never upload their private wholesale margins, supplier costs, or pricing baseline to a closed, centralized cloud database where competitor algorithms could scrape or exploit it. In PricePulse AI, every price check and API key stays sealed in the browser's local sandbox (localStorage).

  3. No Vendor Lock-In:

    The application does not depend on a single proprietary backend. If an API endpoint changes, the open architecture adapts dynamically or runs client-side simulation.

My Agent Session

This project was developed with Google Antigravity AI as an advanced agentic coding partner.

Key milestones achieved during the session:

  • Designed and refined the Retail Defense Pivot: Transitioned technical e-commerce scraping jargon into actionable spoken dialogue for offline retail shopkeepers.
  • Engineered the High-Speed Connection & Auto-Negotiation Engine: Eliminated slow sequential pinging and built dynamic Google Gemini catalog discovery.
  • Solved Anti-Bot Interception for Amazon.in: Built smart URL slug parsers to extract real product names directly from /product-name/dp/ASIN links even when target sites throw robot checks.
  • Enhanced Typography & Accessibility: Designed a high-contrast Light Theme alongside the Dark Mode to guarantee clear visibility under bright store counter lighting.

For pagination SEO, give each result page a real URL and link to the sequence with ordinary crawlable links. Check that page two opens directly, shows its own results, and can lead to later pages. A “Load more” button alone does not establish that a crawler can follow the collection.

This matters when useful public pages sit beyond the first screen of a directory or archive. Before adding more content, test the path that leads to the content you already have. The goal is reliable discovery of relevant pages, not making every possible filtered view eligible for search.

Define the collection you intend to expose

Start with one public collection, such as a directory of integration guides. Write down which detail pages belong in it and which views serve a real reader need. A pagination review should not quietly turn thousands of arbitrary sort and filter combinations into a search strategy.

Use a small hypothetical fixture for the review: 23 directory entries, ten results per page, and three result pages. Number the entries internally so you can compare the sequence. These are test values, not a claim about any live website or an engine's preferred page size.

Decide what a complete pass through that collection means. A reader should be able to reach every included detail page, understand where they are, and move through the list without losing the selected context. Those requirements give the review a clear finish line.

Check the documented discovery behavior

Google's pagination guidance says its crawlers generally follow links in anchor elements with href attributes. They generally do not click buttons that trigger more results. The guide recommends crawlable links between pages in a sequence and a unique URL for each page.

The same guide says each paginated page should have its own canonical URL, rather than pointing every page back to page one. It also advises against using URL fragments for page numbers. Google no longer uses rel="next" and rel="prev" as pagination signals.

Keep the scope of that evidence clear. These are Google's documented practices. They do not establish how every AI crawler handles every framework. A public link path is a sound thing to test, but it is not proof that an answer engine will cite an entry.

Open page two in a fresh tab

Use the actual page-two link from the live interface. Open it in a fresh tab and copy the observed URL into your review notes. Do not start from a URL you invented because the route looks predictable. You are checking what the product actually exposes.

A path such as /guides?page=2 can identify the second page. The exact route format is less important than whether it is stable and represents the intended view. Confirm that the second page shows entries 11 through 20 in the hypothetical fixture, with the same relevant collection context.

Now reload that URL. Try it without first visiting page one. If the results only exist after earlier clicks or session state, the URL is not yet a dependable representation of page two. Record the visible result and the condition that caused it to fail.

Check the rendered title or page label too. A person arriving directly should know this is a later part of a collection. They should have a way to return to the beginning and enough context to understand what the collection contains.

Inspect the path to later entries

From page one, inspect the real next-page control. Is it a link with a destination, or only a button that runs an event handler? Then inspect the control on page two. The first link being crawlable does not establish that the rest of the sequence is connected.

For a load-more interface, ask whether a usable link-based route exists alongside the interaction. You can preserve the reader's preferred browsing experience while giving result pages stable destinations. Review the actual implementation instead of treating a visual button label as evidence.

Follow the sequence to page three. In the fixture, it should contain entries 21 through 23. Open one detail page from each result page. Confirm the links lead to the intended public content rather than a placeholder, sign-in wall, or unrelated redirect.

Record a short path in the review: collection start, second page, last page, and a detail page from each. This makes the finding reproducible. “Deep pages seem hard to find” is much harder for another developer to investigate.

Test the end of the sequence

The final page deserves a separate check. It should not offer a next link that returns the same results forever. A misleading endless sequence wastes a reader's time and makes it harder to tell which URLs represent distinct pages.

Test an out-of-range page using your own site's approved development or review process. Decide with the team what a valid response should be when a requested page no longer exists. The important point is to avoid silently presenting an unrelated page as if the request succeeded.

Also test what happens after the collection changes. If a new entry moves existing items to later pages, can readers still find the relevant detail pages through stable item links? Pagination is a way into the content; it should not be the identity of the content itself.

Review URLs, canonicals, and sort order together

Read the canonical URL on each sampled result page and compare it with the view shown. If every later page declares page one as canonical, record that as a mismatch with Google's pagination guidance. Include both the observed page URL and declared canonical in the issue.

Check that the sort order is defined well enough for the sequence to make sense. If two entries share a sort value, a consistent tie-breaker can prevent confusing movement during a review. This is an implementation recommendation for predictable lists, not a documented search ranking factor.

Keep sorting and filtering separate in your notes. A page number identifies a position within a particular collection state. Losing a required filter when moving to page two changes the question the page answers. Test one supported filtered sequence when that behavior matters to the reader.

Write a fix request another person can verify

A useful issue includes the starting URL, the control used, the destination observed, the expected entries, and the actual result. Add a screenshot when it clarifies the failure. Avoid an issue title such as “Fix SEO” when the defect is a missing destination link.

State an acceptance check in ordinary terms: opening the observed second-page URL directly shows the intended entries; a crawlable link leads to the next valid page; the final page stops the sequence; each sampled detail page opens correctly. The implementation can then be reviewed against visible behavior.

After the fix, repeat the same small sample. Expand the test only if a new failure suggests a wider problem. A focused collection review is easier to maintain than a huge checklist nobody repeats after a routing change.

Keep the outcome honest. You can verify that the pages and links work and that they follow the documented Google guidance you checked. Indexing, organic ranking, and AI citations require separate observations. Making page two findable removes a discovery problem; it does not promise what any engine will do with the content.
