articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

This week I hit two years sober and relaunched my Substack. I wrote the post I'd been waiting two years to write, hit publish, and then realized I wasn't done. I still had to rewrite it as a Substack Note, an Instagram caption, a LinkedIn post and a short post. Each app wants a different length, a different tone, and a different place for the link.

So I built Ripple. You paste a blog post or newsletter, pick your tone, and get four ready-to-post drafts:

  • 📝 Substack Note: 2–4 sentences that make people open the post
  • 📸 Instagram caption: a scroll-stopping first line, emojis, "Link in bio," your sign-off and hashtags
  • 💼 LinkedIn post: a hook, short lines, a question at the end, and the link ready to paste as the first comment
  • 💬 X / Threads / Bluesky: one punchy line that fits in 280 characters, link included

The writing is done by Gemma, running entirely in your browser. Your unpublished post never leaves your device.

Who would pay for it: indie writers, newsletter creators and small business bloggers. Basically anyone who publishes and then dreads the "now share it everywhere" part. There's no server and no API bill, so it can stay cheap: a small monthly subscription, a few dollars, instead of the pricey social media tools.

Demo

Live app: https://ripple-nxxz.onrender.com/
(Chrome or Edge on a laptop works best. Click "Try a sample" if you don't have a post handy.)

Code

tmott13 / ripple

One post, every platform. Turns a blog post into a Substack Note, Instagram caption, LinkedIn post and short post, with Gemma running privately in your browser.

✨ Ripple

One post. Every platform. Written privately in your browser.

Paste a blog post or newsletter and get a Substack Note, an Instagram caption, a LinkedIn post and a short post for X, Threads or Bluesky. The drafts are written by Gemma running in your browser with WebLLM, so your unpublished writing never leaves your device.

Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 2: Side Hustle.

Who it's for

Indie writers, newsletter creators and small business bloggers who publish a post and then spend another hour rewriting it for every app.

How it works

  • Gemma does the writing. Each platform gets its own short, focused prompt, because small models do best with one clear job.
  • The app owns the facts. Gemma never writes links, hashtags or sign-offs. The app adds the link where each platform wants it ("Link in bio" on Instagram, a ready-to-copy first comment…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

  • Open model: Gemma 2 2B (gemma-2-2b-it-q4f16_1-MLC) on laptops, with Gemma 3 1B as the lighter option and the only one that fits on an iPhone.
  • Runs in the browser: WebLLM runs Gemma on the device's GPU with WebGPU. The model downloads once and is cached, so after that it even works offline.
  • Frontend: Angular 22 with signals. Drafts stream in word by word, and everything you type is saved in your browser only.
  • Hosting: a free static site on Render. There's no backend at all.

The most important design decision came from my last project. In Off-Grid Trails, I learned that a small model is great with words and shaky with facts. So in Ripple, Gemma writes the words and the app owns the facts:

  1. Links: Gemma is told not to write links, and the app strips any it sneaks in. Then the app puts your link exactly where each platform wants it.
  2. Hashtags: Gemma suggests topics, and the app turns them into clean hashtags and caps them per platform.
  3. Limits: the app enforces each platform's character limit and cuts at a full sentence, never mid-word. On X, it saves 23 characters for your link.
  4. Made-up numbers: if a draft includes a number that isn't anywhere in your post, the app flags it with a ⚠️ so you can check it before posting. Small models love to invent stats.
  5. Cleanup: "Sure! Here's your caption:" preambles, quote marks and repeated sentences get stripped automatically.

Each platform also gets its own short prompt instead of one giant one. A 2B model does much better with one clear job at a time.

I was surprised by how well Gemma generated the text for the post using the correct tone for each.

I built this with Claude as my pair programmer. I picked the problem from my own week, made the product calls, and tested it on my own posts.

Why Open Innovation Matters

  • Your drafts stay private. Unpublished writing is personal. Mine was about my sobriety. With an open model running locally, nothing is uploaded to anyone's server.
  • It costs nothing to run. There's no per-request API bill, so a side hustle like this can stay cheap for creators.
  • It works offline. Once Gemma is downloaded, you can write your captions on a plane.
  • I control the whole pipeline. I can shrink the model's memory, rewrite the prompts, and add my own safety checks around it. A closed API would be a black box in the middle.

My First User

I was my first user for Ripple. I took my most recent post on my Substack and pasted it in along with the title and URL to the post. I chose "warm" for the tone and my name as the sign-off. I kept all four platforms selected.

Gemma was able to generate four wonderful captions with the correct tone for each platform along with helpful hashtags. I even like the emojis it included in each response.

I like that I can regenerate the text if I don't particularly like or agree with the response.

I don't think I would change anything currently. It works as expected and does an excellent job. I'm so glad I had this idea and to be able to bring it to life! This is definitely a tool I can see myself using and expanding on in the future for my own blogging.

I would pay a small subscription fee per month to use it. I think it is worth it, especially if you write often.

One thing I would add for the future of the app is the ability for Ripple to scrape the article text from the URL so you don't have to paste in the entire article. I probably would also add more social platforms like Facebook, Medium, and Wordpress.

Prize Categories

  • Gemma: Gemma 2 2B and Gemma 3 1B run fully in the browser with WebLLM, and the app is built around keeping their output trustworthy.
  • Render: the app is deployed as a free Render static site from a render.yaml blueprint.

Thanks to DEV, the Hacktoberfest team, and the MLC/WebLLM and Gemma teams for making on-device AI this easy to try. ✨

articles.title: From Messy WhatsApp Chits to GST Invoices in 15s — Local AI with Ollama & Qwen 2.5
articles.description: BahiPilot: The Local-First AI Back Office for Bharat's Wholesalers   This is a submission...
articles.body_html:
BahiPilot: The Local-First AI Back Office for Bharat's Wholesalers

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

Across India's wholesale markets (mandis), billions of dollars in daily trade move not through ERP software, but through informal WhatsApp photos of handwritten paper chits (parchis), voice notes, and loose text messages.

A small grain distributor or FMCG stockist in a tier-2 trade hub typically spends 2 to 3 hours every evening performing tedious, error-prone transcription: deciphering scribbled product abbreviations, checking physical warehouse stock, typing quantities into software, balancing running Khatabook customer ledgers, and printing GST-compliant tax invoices.

BahiPilot (बही पायलट) is an open-source, local-first AI back office built specifically to eliminate this bottleneck for small Indian wholesalers, distributors, and stockists.

What BahiPilot Does:

  1. Multi-Modal Order Ingestion: Accepts messy WhatsApp photos, scanned paper chits, digital PDF invoices, or raw Hinglish text messages.
  2. Local Open-Weight AI Extraction: Uses open-weight models (Qwen 2.5:7b / Llama 3.2) via Ollama to parse messy colloquial text into structured JSON line items—with zero marginal token cost and complete data privacy.
  3. Deterministic Catalogue & Alias Matching: Reconciles vernacular terms ("10 bori Basmati Rice 25kg", "5 carton Fortune Oil", "20 pkt Tata Salt") against the business catalogue using token-overlap fuzzy matching and alias indexing.
  4. Human-in-the-Loop Review: Provides an interactive 4-stage review screen where quantities, unit rates, and customer accounts can be reviewed with ambiguity warning flags before anything is committed.
  5. Strict Financial Integrity (Zero LLM Math): All subtotals, GST (CGST/SGST/IGST), discount deductions, and totals are computed strictly server-side using Python Decimal (paise precision). The LLM is never allowed to hallucinate financial figures.
  6. Atomic Ledger & Stock Commitment: Zero stock is deducted and zero customer ledger entries are written until the business owner explicitly clicks Approve. Cancellation atomically restores inventory and balances the customer's running ledger.
  7. GST-Ready Printable Invoices & Khatabook: Generates clean, printable B2B tax invoices with HSN breakdowns, and maintains a running chronological customer statement with real-time UPI and cash payment recording.

Who Would Pay for It?

Small and medium distributors, grain wholesalers (Arhatiyas), and FMCG stockists handling 30 to 200 orders a day. They operate on thin 2%–5% gross margins and currently either hire data entry clerks (costing ₹15,000–₹25,000/month) or lose hours of their own family time every night balancing paper Bahi Khata ledgers. A private, local back office that cuts transcription time by 80% pays for itself in days.

Demo

  • 🎥 Video Walkthrough: Check out our step-by-step video demo showcasing WhatsApp chit ingestion, catalogue reconciliation, atomic approval, and GST invoice printing.

Code

srijan-0-7 / hacktoberfest-dev-2

BahiPilot (बही पायलट)

Local-First AI Back Office for Small Indian Wholesalers & Distributors

BahiPilot streamlines wholesale and distribution operations across Bharat: ingest messy handwritten chits, WhatsApp order screenshots, and PDF invoices; convert them into structured line items using local open-weight AI (Ollama) or Gemini API; reconcile against catalogue and available stock; and execute transactional inventory deduction, customer ledger posting, and GST-ready invoice printing.

🌟 Key Features

  1. Dual AI Order Ingestion (Flagship 4-Stage Guided Workflow):

    • Stage 1 (Input): Upload invoices/receipts (PNG, JPEG, PDF) or paste informal order text (Hinglish/English chits, e.g., "10 bori Basmati Rice 25kg, 5 carton Fortune Oil 1L, 20 packet Tata Salt").
    • Stage 2 (Extraction): Extracts text via PyMuPDF or Tesseract OCR, prompts local LLMs (Ollama qwen2.5:7b / llama3.2) or Google Gemini (gemini-2.5-flash), strictly adhering to structured JSON schemas.
    • Stage 3 (Review & Reconcile): Interactive review table matching extracted aliases…
View on GitHub

Repository: https://github.com/srijan-0-7/hacktoberfest-dev-2

Architecture Highlights:

  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS (custom Midnight Navy & Emerald Green theme), TanStack Query v5, Recharts, Lucide Icons.
  • Backend: Python 3.11+, FastAPI, Pydantic v2, SQLAlchemy 2.0, SQLite (with WAL mode & strict PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON).
  • AI Engine: Pluggable provider architecture:
    • Local primary: Ollama REST provider (qwen2.5:7b / llama3.2)
    • Cloud fallback: Google Gemini API (gemini-3.8-flash)
  • Document Processing: PyMuPDF (fitz) for native PDF stream extraction, Pillow for preprocessing, and optional Tesseract OCR.
  • Production Ready: Pre-configured Dockerfile (multi-stage build) and render.yaml for 1-click cloud deployment.

How I Built It

1. Dual AI Provider with Structured Pydantic Schemas

BahiPilot implements an extensible BaseAIProvider interface. The prompt strictly limits the LLM's task to linguistic extraction, injecting the business's real catalogue and customer list as context:

class ExtractionRawLLMOutput(BaseModel):
    customer_name: Optional[str] = None
    items: List[RawItemExtraction] = Field(default_factory=list)
    notes: List[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
    overall_needs_review: bool = True

By requesting structured JSON output and validating via Pydantic schemas, we eliminate hallucinated formats while handling diverse vernacular inputs (Hinglish, mixed English/Hindi names, informal units).

2. Deterministic Alias & Catalogue Matcher

In Indian trade, the same product is called ten different names: "Chawal", "Basmati 25kg", "Rice bag", or "India Gate Classic".

Instead of trusting an LLM to guess database foreign keys, BahiPilot uses a tiered deterministic matching algorithm:

  1. Exact SKU and Product Name normalization
  2. Exact Alias array lookup
  3. Token coverage & overlap ratios: 
# Query coverage: what percentage of the requested item's words exist in this product?
overlap = query_tokens.intersection(prod_tokens)
query_coverage = len(overlap) / len(query_tokens)
jaccard = len(overlap) / len(query_tokens.union(prod_tokens))
score = max(query_coverage * 0.82, jaccard)

Unmatched or low-confidence items are surfaced with visual warning badges on the review screen, forcing human-in-the-loop resolution before committing to stock.

3. Strict Server-Side Financial Math & Transactional State

To guarantee financial trust:

  • Zero arithmetic is performed by the LLM. Line subtotals, CGST/SGST splits, and grand totals are calculated with Python Decimal in paise accuracy.
  • Orders start in DRAFT or PENDING_REVIEW. Stock deduction and ledger postings execute only upon explicit user APPROVE action in an atomic database transaction. If cancelled, an automated stock restoration and ledger debit reversal is logged.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open-source and open-weight AI are not just philosophical preferences for Bharat's MSMEs—they are economic and operational necessities:

  1. Zero Marginal Inference Cost:

    Proprietary cloud APIs charging per token or per image are economically unfeasible for small businesses operating on 2%–4% margins. A distributor processing 150 chits a day would face unpredictable recurring monthly SaaS bills. With open-weight models like Qwen 2.5 running on a basic local shop desktop via Ollama, marginal inference cost is exactly ₹0.00.

  2. Absolute Data Sovereignty & Confidentiality:

    Indian wholesalers guard their customer directories, negotiated volume discounts, and turnover numbers as core trade secrets. Small business owners are rightfully wary of transmitting unredacted order photos and customer lists to third-party cloud servers. Local open weights keep 100% of the data inside the four walls of the shop.

  3. Offline Continuity in Trade Mandis:

    Wholesale grain and spice markets often suffer from spotty mobile networks and intermittent broadband. Because BahiPilot's inference and database run entirely on localhost, the distributor can continue scanning orders, adjusting stock, and issuing invoices even when the internet is completely down.

  4. Open Vocabulary & Model Independence:

    Open weights can be fine-tuned or prompt-engineered for regional Indian languages (Hindi, Marathi, Gujarati, Tamil) and unique market jargon without vendor lock-in or fear of arbitrary API deprecation.

My Agent Session

This entire project was architected, implemented, and debugged through an end-to-end AI pair programming session using Antigravity.

Key milestones accomplished during the agent session:

  • System Architecture & Domain Modeling: Engineered the SQLite multi-table schema (customers, products, orders, order_items, ledger_entries) with strict foreign keys and transactional consistency.
  • Dual AI Provider Integration: Built the pluggable BaseAIProvider abstraction supporting local Ollama (qwen2.5:7b / llama3.2) and Gemini cloud fallback with structured JSON validation via Pydantic v2.
  • Deterministic Token-Overlap Matcher: Developed the fuzzy alias matching engine to reconcile colloquial Indian trade terms ("10 bori Basmati Rice", "5 carton Fortune Oil") with catalogue items at 85%–95% confidence without calling external APIs.
  • Full-Stack Polish & Verification: Created the responsive React 19 + Tailwind CSS frontend, wired TanStack Query endpoints, resolved Vite URL routing, and verified atomic approval, inventory deduction, and GST invoice generation.

My First User

To ground BahiPilot in reality, I tested the order import pipeline with Ramesh Gupta, who operates a wholesale grocery and provisions store (Gupta Kirana & Provisions) supplying 45 retail kirana shops in Maharashtra.

What He Tested:

Ramesh pasted a typical evening WhatsApp order list sent by one of his regular buyers:

"10 bori Basmati Rice 25kg, 5 carton Fortune Oil 1L, 20 pkt Tata Salt, 15 packet Maggi. Urgent delivery by 4 PM."

What Happened:

  1. BahiPilot automatically recognized the buyer (Gupta Kirana General Stores) and matched all 4 products against his catalogue inventory with 85%–95% confidence.
  2. The system flagged that his catalogue unit for Maggi was a 24-pack box, allowing him to verify the pack size with one click.
  3. Upon clicking Approve, the stock deducted from his digital godown, the invoice was posted to the buyer's running ledger, and a GST-compliant print bill was ready in under 15 seconds.

His Feedback:

"Every evening after 8 PM, I sit with a notebook and spend an hour and a half making bills and checking who owes how much. If this software can take my WhatsApp orders and prepare my bills and Khatabook without needing an internet connection, it saves me at least 10 hours a week. I don't want my customer rates going to foreign clouds, so keeping it on my shop laptop is a huge relief."

Prize Categories

  • Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle (Main Category)

Tech Stack Summary

  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vite, TanStack Query
  • Backend: FastAPI, Pydantic v2, SQLAlchemy, SQLite
  • AI Models: Ollama (qwen2.5:7b), Google Gemini API (gemini-3.8-flash)
  • Document Processing: PyMuPDF, Pillow, Tesseract OCR
  • Deployment: Docker, Render Blueprint (render.yaml), Localtunnel

Built with ❤️ for Indian MSMEs and the open-source AI community.

articles.title: One Rust Unicode Bug, Three Coding Models: A Reproducible Comparison
articles.description: Coding-model leaderboards reveal little about how a model handles a real bug. A Rust function can...
articles.body_html:
Coding-model leaderboards reveal little about how a model handles a real bug. A Rust function can work on ASCII and still panic on valid Unicode because it slices UTF-8 at the wrong byte boundary. The fix must respect character boundaries and preserve the &str return type. This article uses one reproducible bug, one prompt, and the same regression tests to compare three models on the quality of their patches, not the confidence of their explanations.

A one-line Rust slice can panic on valid UTF-8. That makes it a useful coding-model challenge. The fix must preserve the function signature, handle character boundaries, and pass regression tests. This comparison uses the same bug for three models and judges their patches using compiler output rather than leaderboard scores.

The bug

The function below is supposed to return the first n characters of a string. It works on plain ASCII and panics when n cuts through a multibyte UTF-8 character.

pub fn prefix(input: &str, n: usize) -> &str {
    if n >= input.len() {
        return input;
    }
    &input[..n]
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::prefix;

    #[test]
    fn ascii() {
        assert_eq!(prefix("rustacean", 4), "rust");
    }

    #[test]
    fn unicode() {
        assert_eq!(prefix("café", 4), "café");
    }

    #[test]
    fn beyond_length() {
        assert_eq!(prefix("é", 10), "é");
    }
}

The original implementation counts bytes, not characters. In UTF-8, the final é in café occupies two bytes. Slicing at byte index four cuts through that character and panics. Save the code as src/lib.rs in a new Cargo library project. Run cargo test to reproduce the failing Unicode case.

Three models, one task

The three candidates are DeepSeek V4 Pro, Claude Fable 5.1, and Grok Build 0.1. These are the target model pages for the comparison. Model availability, exact API identifiers, and supported parameters must be checked against the live catalog before execution.

Model API identifier Temperature Input Version
DeepSeek V4 Pro Confirm from catalog 0 Same Rust file and prompt Record API version
Claude Fable 5.1 Confirm from catalog 0 Same Rust file and prompt Record API version
Grok Build 0.1 Confirm from catalog 0 Same Rust file and prompt Record API version

Use the same request body, system instructions, maximum output allowance, and test environment for every model. Record the exact model ID returned by the API. A zero temperature reduces randomness but does not guarantee identical answers on repeated calls.

The prompt

Use the following prompt unchanged for every model.

Fix the Rust function below. It must return the first n Unicode scalar values without panicking. Keep the return type &str. Explain the bug briefly, return a complete src/lib.rs, and add a regression test for an emoji and a combining character. Do not add external dependencies.

Append the entire original src/lib.rs after that instruction. Do not tell one model about another model's failure. Do not silently repair a response before testing.

What to inspect in each model's patch

DeepSeek V4 Pro

Capture the raw response, its reported input and output tokens, the elapsed request time, and the first cargo test output. A correct patch should iterate over char boundaries rather than slice at an arbitrary byte index. If the returned code does not compile, retain the error and count the next prompt as another attempt. Add a screenshot of the response and terminal output from the actual run.

Claude Fable 5.1

Use the identical source and prompt. Record whether the model preserves the borrowed &str return type and whether it handles a request longer than the character count. Check the combining-character case carefully. Unicode scalar values are not the same as grapheme clusters. A request for one scalar value from an e followed by a combining accent may return only the e. That is correct under this task's definition.

Grok Build 0.1

Repeat the procedure without editing the prompt. Review whether the model changes the API, introduces a dependency, or returns a String instead of &str. These changes matter even when the visible output looks correct. Keep the first attempt and any follow-up attempts as separate records.

What a correct fix looks like

One valid approach uses char_indices to find the byte boundary after the requested number of scalar values.

pub fn prefix(input: &str, n: usize) -> &str {
    let end = input
        .char_indices()
        .nth(n)
        .map(|(index, _)| index)
        .unwrap_or(input.len());
    &input[..end]
}

This reference implementation is a correctness oracle for the exercise, not an attributed output from any model. The test suite should include ASCII, multibyte characters, empty strings, n equal to zero, n greater than the character count, emoji, and decomposed accents. The reference code should be kept out of model prompts.

Comparison scorecard

Model First attempt passes Attempts Wall time Input tokens Output tokens Notes
DeepSeek V4 Pro Enter from cargo test Enter from logs Enter from logs Enter from API Enter from API Compiler and behavior notes
Claude Fable 5.1 Enter from cargo test Enter from logs Enter from logs Enter from API Enter from API Compiler and behavior notes
Grok Build 0.1 Enter from cargo test Enter from logs Enter from logs Enter from API Enter from API Compiler and behavior notes

The scorecard becomes useful once each row is populated from the first response, Cargo output, and API logs. Until then, it is a repeatable evaluation worksheet rather than a model ranking.

What to pick for each coding task

For short patches, first-pass compilation and correct edge cases matter more than a polished explanation. For larger refactors, examine how often a model changes unrelated code. For code review, test whether it identifies the byte-versus-character distinction without prompting. For terminal automation, compare how predictably each model follows the required output format.

The best LLM for coding is task dependent. One Rust bug cannot establish which model performs best across a whole repository, language, or toolchain. It can reveal whether a model handles a concrete failure mode under controlled conditions.

How to repeat the comparison

Create a Cargo library with cargo new unicode-prefix --lib. Replace src/lib.rs with the buggy example and run cargo test. Send the same prompt and file to each confirmed model identifier. Save the raw JSON response, request timestamp, token usage fields, and model version. Extract the proposed code into a clean working tree for each attempt. Run cargo fmt --check, cargo test, and cargo clippy. Record failures without modifying the first answer.

Keep the repository organized as follows:

baseline/src/lib.rs
oracle/src/lib.rs
prompts/task.txt
runs/<model>/response.json
runs/<model>/cargo-test.txt

Publish a repository link only after the files are uploaded. The reproducible artifact is the code and logs, not a ranking graphic.

A shareable comparison includes the repository, unedited first responses, and Cargo logs. Readers can inspect both the proposed fixes and the failures.

articles.title: How I finally understood what idempotency is
articles.description: The Intro   Idempotency. Eight letters, five syllables, and a word I pretended to understand...
articles.body_html:
The Intro

Idempotency. Eight letters, five syllables, and a word I pretended to understand in meetings for an embarrassingly long time.

It kept showing up in API docs, in Stripe's dashboard, in that one coworker's code review comments. I nodded. I did not know.

So today we are going to build the bug that makes idempotency matter, charge a fake customer twice, and then fix it. By the end, "idempotent" will be a word you can use in a sentence without sweating.

The What

Here is the dictionary version:

An operation is idempotent if performing it multiple times has the same effect as performing it once.

That's it. No, really, that's the whole concept. The hard part is noticing where it matters.

My favorite non-code example: the elevator button. Press it once, the elevator comes. Press it twelve times because you are late... the elevator still comes once. The button is idempotent. Impatient people everywhere rely on this.

Now compare that to a vending machine button. Press it twice and you get two sodas and one empty wallet. Not idempotent.

Most of your app is an elevator button. Some of it is a vending machine. The trouble starts when a vending machine gets pressed twice by accident.

The How

Let's build a tiny "pay for an order" endpoint with Express and TypeScript. One route, one fake payment provider, zero databases:

// src/server.ts
import express from 'express'

const app = express()
app.use(express.json())

const orders = new Map<string, { total: number; paid: boolean }>()
orders.set('ord_1', { total: 50, paid: false })

async function chargeCard(amount: number) {
  console.log(`💳 charged $${amount}`)
  return `ch_${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 8)}`
}

app.post('/orders/:id/pay', async (req, res) => {
  const order = orders.get(req.params.id)
  if (!order) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'order not found' })

  const chargeId = await chargeCard(order.total)
  order.paid = true

  res.json({ chargeId })
})

app.listen(3000, () => console.log('listening on :3000'))

Start it with npx tsx src/server.ts and pay for the order:

curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay

💳 charged $50

Lovely. Fifty bucks, one charge, everyone's happy. 🎉

Now let's be realistic about the internet. Your frontend sends the request, the server charges the card, and then... the Wi-Fi hiccups. The response never arrives. The frontend (or the HTTP client, or the user mashing the button) does what every client does when it sees a timeout: it retries.

curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay
curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay

💳 charged $50
💳 charged $50

Two charges. One order. One customer opening a support ticket with a lot of capital letters. 😬

Our endpoint is a vending machine. Every press costs money. And notice that the client did nothing wrong, retrying on a timeout is the correct thing to do. The endpoint just wasn't ready for it.

Step 1: look before you charge

The cheapest fix is to make the endpoint check its own state first:

app.post('/orders/:id/pay', async (req, res) => {
  const order = orders.get(req.params.id)
  if (!order) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'order not found' })

  if (order.paid) {
    return res.json({ chargeId: order.chargeId, alreadyPaid: true })
  }

  const chargeId = await chargeCard(order.total)
  order.paid = true
  order.chargeId = chargeId

  res.json({ chargeId })
})

(Add chargeId?: string to the order type so TypeScript stops yelling.)

Run the double curl again:

💳 charged $50

One charge. The second request got a polite "yep, already done" with the same chargeId as the first. Press the elevator button all you want now.

That's idempotency in one if. The operation "pay order 1" now has the same result whether you call it once or five hundred times.

Step 2: the sneaky gap

Before you ship, let's be honest about a hole. What if the two requests arrive at the same time? Both read paid === false, both charge, both set paid = true. Our if didn't help.

In a real app with a real database you close that gap by making the "check and mark" step atomic. In Postgres that's something like:

UPDATE orders SET paid = true WHERE id = $1 AND paid = false

If that update touches one row, you won the race, go charge the card. If it touches zero rows, someone else got there first, return their result. Same idea as our if, just one that the database enforces so two requests can't both pass.

Step 3: idempotency keys (the grown-up version)

There's one more case the paid flag can't cover: what if the client legitimately wants to pay twice? Say, two different orders that happen to look identical, or a "buy again" button.

The industry answer is an idempotency key. The client generates a random ID per attempt and sends it in a header. The server remembers which keys it has seen:

const seen = new Map<string, unknown>()

app.post('/orders/:id/pay', async (req, res) => {
  const key = req.header('Idempotency-Key')
  if (!key) return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Idempotency-Key header required' })

  if (seen.has(key)) {
    return res.json(seen.get(key))
  }

  const order = orders.get(req.params.id)
  if (!order) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'order not found' })

  const chargeId = await chargeCard(order.total)
  order.paid = true

  const response = { chargeId }
  seen.set(key, response)
  res.json(response)
})

curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123"
curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123"

💳 charged $50

Same key, one charge, identical response both times. A retry is now safe by design: the client keeps the same key while retrying, and only generates a new one when it genuinely wants a new action.

This is exactly what Stripe, PayPal and friends ask you to send. Now you know why. 🧠

(In production, seen lives in your database or Redis with an expiry, not in a Map. But the shape is the same.)

Step 4: wait, we trust the client to pick the key?

Yep. And it has to be that way. Look at it from the server's side: two identical POST /orders/ord_1/pay requests show up. Is that a flaky network resending one payment, or a customer who genuinely wants to buy twice? The server has no idea. Only the thing that decided to pay knows if it's deciding again. So the client tags the decision, and retries carry the same tag.

What we don't do is trust the client blindly. The server adds a few guardrails:

  • Scope the key to the user. Look it up as (userId, key), not just key. Nobody can replay or collide with someone else's request.
  • Fingerprint the body. Store a hash of the request along with the key. Same key, different body? That's not a retry, that's someone being clever. Answer with a 422.
  • Expire keys. Keep them for a day or so, then forget them. A retry from last month is not a retry.
  • Lock while in flight. If a second request with the same key arrives while the first is still running, make it wait (or return a 409). That also closes the race from Step 2.

With those four, the client can only ever use a key to say "that same thing again, please". Which is exactly what we wanted.

The Why

Let's zoom out, because this is bigger than payments:

  • Retries are everywhere. HTTP clients retry. Message queues redeliver. Users double-click. Cron jobs overlap. If your operation isn't idempotent, every one of those is a bug waiting for a bad Wi-Fi day.
  • Idempotent code is restartable code. A script that imports 10,000 rows and crashes at row 7,000? If each row is an "insert or update", you just run it again. If it's "insert", you now have 7,000 duplicates and a long afternoon.
  • HTTP already has opinions. GET, PUT and DELETE are supposed to be idempotent. POST is not. That's why "create order" is a POST and "set order status" is a PUT. Delete something twice and the second call should say "fine, it's gone" rather than crash.
  • It's a design question, not a library. No package makes your code idempotent. You get it by asking, for every action: "what happens if this runs twice?" and making the answer "nothing new".

The one-sentence version to keep in your pocket: pressing it again should never make things worse.

The Goodbye

Next time someone drops "we should make that idempotent" in a review, you can nod and know. Even better, you can go find the endpoint in your app that charges, emails or creates something, run it twice, and see what happens.

Go press some elevator buttons. Happy coding 🤝

articles.title: An ESP32 and a Local Vision Model Drive My iPhone
articles.description: Apple spent 17 years convincing us that controlling an iPhone requires Xcode, a $99 developer...
articles.body_html:
Apple spent 17 years convincing us that controlling an iPhone requires Xcode, a $99 developer account, and a that costs more than your couch.

Henry Yuan spent $7 to prove them wrong.

His repo — esp32-iphone-agent — showed up on my timeline October 11th as a 12-star MIT-licensed shitpost: "A $7 ESP32 lets an AI agent control a stock iPhone." Hackaday picked it up Oct 14th. By the time I cloned it, it had 2,975 stars. You are still early.

The trick isn't AI. It's hardware heresy.

Yuan split the classic computer-use agent into three organs and built each from spare parts:

  • Eyes: AirPlay mirroring
  • Hands: An ESP32-S3 pretending to be a USB mouse and keyboard
  • Brain: Any OpenAI-compatible vision endpoint

No WebDriverAgent. No CoreDevice hack. No app on the phone that Apple has to sign. Just a microcontroller that your iPhone already trusts because, to iOS, it looks like a mouse.

I rebuilt it the way a solo maker would actually run it: not on two DGX Sparks running Qwen3-VL-Flash like Henry did for the demo, but on one consumer GPU with Ollama and a 7B vision model. And because the README hand-waves past the scariest part, I'm going to talk about the security model, because what we just built is literally a Wi-Fi-controlled USB HID implant.

This is the teardown.

1. The Eyes: UxPlay plus a GStreamer JPEG pipeline

The original v0.1.0 architecture — which is what most of us will still build because it's simpler to debug — is beautiful in a junkyard way.

iPhone → (Wi-Fi) AirPlay → Mac/Linux box running UxPlay → GStreamer → JPEGs → your agent.

Yuan's Hackaday writeup puts it plainly: screen mirroring is captured with UxPlay, then "a Gstreamer pipeline is then used to feed the screen as a JPEG stream to the AI agent of your choice."

On my Linux box:
UxPlay is the unsung hero here. It's a real AirPlay receiver built on GStreamer plugins, emulating an . Your iPhone thinks it's just projecting to a TV. In the new firmware, Yuan went even more feral: the ESP32-S3 itself opens its own hotspot called ESP32 Agent and is the AirPlay receiver, passing H.264 through to an iPhone app over BLE. The phone keeps cellular data for the model while its Wi-Fi is held hostage.

Either way, you get what no Xcode automation gives you: the real framebuffer. Not a screenshot API, the actual rendered screen at ∼5 fps, 480x1040. Low enough to keep BLE happy, high enough for a VLM to read.

My GStreamer pipeline for the legacy rig:
Feed that into /api/v1/chat/completions as base64 images. That's your eyes.

2. The Hands: ESP32-S3 as USB HID, and why AssistiveTouch is the trick

Here's the bit that made me grin out loud.

Apple will never let a random USB device tap the screen. But it will let an accessibility mouse move a cursor. Turn on AssistiveTouch, plug in a USB mouse, and iOS draws a little pointer you can drag around. Tap = click. Swipe = drag.

Yuan's firmware does exactly that: the board is a standard USB mouse and keyboard. With AssistiveTouch on, the mouse moves an on-screen pointer, so a click is a tap and a drag is a swipe.

I flashed a Seeed XIAO ESP32S3 — plain version, 8MB PSRAM, not Sense, not Plus, about $7. Any ESP32-S3 with native USB and PSRAM works. iOS 18+, USB-C plugs straight in, Lightning needs that cursed $30 Camera Adapter.

Toolchain:
The board exposes two HID interfaces via TinyUSB: relative mouse + ASCII keyboard. The computer tells it over Wi-Fi (legacy) or BLE (new version) to do move x y / click / type "hello". It does.

The genius: pointer drift. Because the mouse is relative, every move accumulates error. Yuan's app tracks it, re-homes it in a corner, and before a precise tap it wiggles the pointer, finds it on screen, and corrects the miss. That wiggle is why my automation stopped missing the tiny x in Safari.

3. Swapping the DGX Sparks for Ollama on one consumer GPU

The README is honest: "The project was developed with nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 served on two DGX Sparks (TensorFold)." Cool if you have $20k lying around.

My maker stack:

  • Host: M2 MacBook Air + RTX 4060 eGPU, or just a 4070 laptop
  • Server: ollama serve or llama.cpp --server with vision
  • Model: qwen2.5vl:7b or minicpm-v:2.6. Qwen is more spatially accurate, MiniCPM is faster.
  • API: Any OpenAI-compatible chat API that accepts images: a cloud API or your own server In the iPhone app you set a separate planner and actor model — and you should, on one GPU. I run Qwen2.5VL 7B as actor (fast taps) and Qwen2-VL 32B quantized on the cloud as planner when I'm on Wi-Fi, or same 7B with a longer system prompt locally.

Per-action latency on local 7B, measured from JPEG in to HID command out:

  • Eyes (AirPlay → JPEG): 180-250ms
  • Vision inference (Ollama 7B Q4_K_M on RTX 4060): 1.8-2.4s
  • Hands (Wi-Fi → USB HID → pointer settle): 350-600ms
  • Screen settle wait: 800ms

Total: ∼3.5 seconds per step. Cloud GPT-4o does it in 1.2s but leaks your banking screen to OpenAI. Local is slower, but it's yours. BLE carries about 300-500 kbps, so the screen is mirrored small (480x1040, ≤5 fps); each step takes a few seconds, most of it the model — that's not a bug, it's physics.

4. Planner vs Actor: One model or two

Yuan ships with two prompts in prompts/ — plain text, bundled with the app, edit them, rebuild, done.

This matters more than you think.

  • One-model setup: One VLM gets "Goal: set alarm 8am Mon/Tue. Current screen:. What action?" It outputs {"action":"tap", "x":512, "y":1340}. Simple, but it forgets why it tapped after 6 steps and loops.[jpeg]
  • Two-model setup: A planner (bigger, slower) says "Step 1: open Clock app. Step 2: tap Alarm. Step 3:..." The actor (smaller, faster) only executes step 2 given the current screen. This is how Yuan's app runs: decode → vision model → action — a planner and an actor: tap, swipe, draw, type, press keys, go home, finish

On one GPU, run the planner every 3 steps, not every step. Cache the plan. The actor fails less when it has a short horizon.

My prompt diff that fixed stuck loops:

"If the screen didn't change after your last action, you MISSED. Wiggle pointer, increase tap radius by 20px, or swipe instead. Never repeat identical coordinates."

Add a change-detector: after each action wait for screen to settle and tell the model whether anything changed. If image_diff < 2%, force a re-plan.

5. Latency and Failure Loops: Calibration, Re-plans, Stuck States

Real talk: this rig fails hilariously.

Failure modes I logged over 50 tasks:

  1. Calibration drift: After 10 taps, pointer is 30px off. Fix: Yuan's app re-homes in corner every 5 actions and wiggles before precise taps. Replicate that. Don't trust absolute coordinates — the device screen's width / height, stored with a calibration is relative.

  2. iOS black holes: iOS does not mirror some screens (passcode entry, Apple Pay, DRM video); mirroring stops when phone locks. Your agent goes blind. You need a timeout that pauses the run and resumes from same step when link returns.

  3. Keyboard hell: Keyboard input is ASCII only. Want to type Chinese? Nope. It types via USB keyboard events, so you get what a US keyboard sends.

  4. Stuck states: Model sees "Alarm set" toggle and thinks it's done, but didn't hit Save. Add a finish action that only planner can call, and require two consecutive finish votes.

My fix loop:
Every run is kept on phone: replay step by step with taps drawn on top, export trace for analysis. Use it.

6. The Threat Model: What this proves about Wi-Fi-controlled HID implants

The README says "Only automate devices and accounts you own." It should say in bigger font: this is a BadUSB with a radio.

You plugged a $7 board into your iPhone that:

  • Is powered by the phone
  • Emulates mouse + keyboard (so it can type anywhere, even in password fields)
  • Runs a Wi-Fi hotspot that your phone auto-joins, with its own AirPlay receiver stack (GPL-3.0 part)
  • Accepts BLE commands to drive that HID, with firmware you flashed via flash.sh

In the legacy version, commands came over Wi-Fi from a Python server. In the new version, it's BLE from an app, but the board still controls HID. If that BLE characteristic isn't authenticated with a rolling secret — and NimBLE-Arduino defaults aren't — anyone within 10m can tell your phone to start typing.

This links directly to your hardware implant work. A Seeed XIAO is the exact form factor for a drop implant: sits inline in a charging cable, looks like a dongle, powered forever, air-gapped from the network except for the hotspot it creates. Apple trusts it because it's HID. iOS AssistiveTouch is an accessibility feature, not a security boundary.

Defenses:

  • Flash with secrets.h changed, enable NimBLE secure connections
  • Never leave board plugged in unattended
  • iOS: Settings → Accessibility → Touch → AssistiveTouch → Devices → forget when done
  • If you're building this for red-team: log that AirPlay mirroring doesn't capture passcode/ Apple Pay — you won't get Secure Enclave screens, but you will get everything else

Yuan did responsible disclosure: repo has SECURITY.md and responsible use note. But the point stands: iPhone automation without Xcode also means iPhone exploitation without Xcode.

BOM for the solo build (what I actually used):

  • Seeed XIAO ESP32S3 (∼$7)
  • Lightning-to-USB Camera Adapter if you're on older iPhone (∼$30)
  • Mac or Linux host, arduino-cli + ESP32 core 3.x, UxPlay, python venv
  • Ollama or llama.cpp with a vision model — I benchmarked qwen2.5vl:7b

Total cost if you own a GPU: $7. Total time: an afternoon of flashing, calibrating, and watching a robot try to set an alarm and fail three times before getting it.

If you want the offline-first LLM scripting part that makes this actually usable — the Ollama prompt engineering, the planner/actor split, the tool calling that doesn't leak screens to the cloud — that's exactly what my guide teaches:

[Aider + OpenClaw: Offline-First AI Scripting, $39.99 — gum.co/l/ggwux]

It covers how to serve any OpenAI-compatible vision endpoint locally, how to write the re-plan loop, and how to export traces for review — the boring stuff that turns a demo into a daily driver.

Apple built a walled garden. We just found the mouse hole.

articles.title: OpenPilot vs Cursor, Cline and Continue: an honest comparison (from the person who built OpenPilot)
articles.description: I'm the solo dev behind OpenPilot, an open-source desktop agent that runs on whatever model you give...
articles.body_html:
I'm the solo dev behind OpenPilot, an open-source desktop agent that runs on whatever model you give it. People keep asking how it compares to Cursor, Cline and Continue, so here's my best attempt at a fair answer. I'm obviously biased, so I've stuck to things you can check in each project's own docs or code, and I've linked them. Where another tool is better, I say so.

Everything below was checked on October 17, 2026. These tools change fast, so if something is out of date, tell me in the comments and I'll fix it.

The short version

  • Cursor is the most polished experience: a full editor with Tab completion, cloud agents and its own models. It's proprietary, and on the Free and Plus plans you can't use your own API keys or third-party models.
  • Cline is the most capable open-source option. It's Apache-2.0 and ships as a VS Code extension, a JetBrains plugin, a CLI and an early desktop app. It works with basically any provider, including Ollama and LM Studio. If you want open source and maximum features, start there.
  • Continue was a pioneering open-source assistant, but its repo is now read-only and no longer actively maintained, after a final 2.0.0 release.
  • OpenPilot is a small, chat-first desktop app (MIT, Electron). You point it at a folder, bring any OpenAI-compatible model, and approve what it runs. It's simpler and much younger than the others, and it's a one-person project.

Side by side

Cursor Cline Continue OpenPilot
License Proprietary Apache-2.0 (JetBrains plugin not open-sourced) Apache-2.0 MIT
Form factor Full editor VS Code ext, JetBrains plugin, CLI, desktop app (v0.0.x), SDK VS Code ext, JetBrains plugin, CLI Standalone desktop app (Electron)
Bring your own key Yes, on Premium and above (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Azure, Bedrock); not on Free/Plus Yes Yes Yes, it's the only way it works
Local models (Ollama / LM Studio) Not among the documented BYOK providers Yes Yes Yes (Ollama preset; LM Studio via custom base URL)
Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint Not documented for BYOK Yes Yes Yes
Approval before commands/edits Has agent review and security settings (see their docs) Yes, every edit and command by default, with auto-approve available — Yes for shell commands, file writes and edits: Deny / Allow / Allow all for this session
Undo / checkpoints — Yes (checkpoints) — No. Use git
Tab autocomplete Yes (Cursor's own models, even with BYOK) — Yes No
MCP Yes Yes Yes Yes
Maintained Yes Yes, very active No, read-only repo Yes (solo)
Price Free tier, paid from $8/mo Free (you pay your model provider) Free Free (you pay your model provider, or nothing with local models)

Sources: Cursor BYOK docs, Cursor plans, Cline README, Continue README and docs, OpenPilot source.

A "—" means I couldn't confirm it from official docs. Please don't read it as "no".

Cursor

Cursor is a full editor, and it's genuinely good at being one: Tab completion, Plan Mode, cloud agents, code review and a long list of integrations. Its BYOK docs are clear about the trade-offs.

  • Supported key providers are OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Azure OpenAI and AWS Bedrock.
  • Custom keys only work for chat models. Tab keeps using Cursor's built-in models.
  • Requests are routed through Cursor's servers for final prompt building, even with your own key. Cursor says the key isn't stored.
  • On the current plans table, Free and Plus don't include third-party models or your own API keys. Premium ($30/mo) and up do.

If you're happy inside Cursor and paying for a plan that fits, I honestly don't think you need OpenPilot. Where it's a poor fit is if you want to run a model on your own machine, use a provider that isn't on that list, or keep requests from passing through a third-party backend.

Cline

Cline is what I'd recommend to most people asking for "open-source Cursor". It runs in VS Code and JetBrains, as a CLI (npm i -g cline), and now as a desktop app. Its features include:

  • Plan and Act modes
  • Checkpoints, so you can undo the agent's work
  • Diffs you can review
  • Linter and compiler awareness
  • Rules and skills, MCP and plugins
  • Multi-agent teams and scheduled agents
  • A huge provider list: Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, OpenRouter, Bedrock, Vertex, Groq, Ollama, LM Studio and any OpenAI-compatible API

By default it asks before every file edit and terminal command, and you can switch on auto-approve.

Compared with that, OpenPilot is a much smaller tool. Cline's desktop app is newer (v0.0.x at the time of writing), but the project overall is far more mature than mine.

Continue

Continue deserves credit for pushing open-source, any-model coding assistants early. As of now, its README says the continuedev/continue repository is no longer actively maintained and is read-only. The team shipped a final 2.0.0 of the VS Code extension, CLI and JetBrains plugin, and that release also removed anonymous telemetry. You can still install it, but don't expect fixes.

OpenPilot: what it actually is

I built OpenPilot because I wanted a Cursor-style agent where I pick the model, including local ones, without living inside a particular editor. In practice:

  • It's a desktop chat app. You add one or more models with a name, a base URL and a key. There are presets for OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Groq, Together, Mistral, xAI, MiniMax and Ollama, or you can use any custom OpenAI-compatible URL. You can switch models per chat.
  • You pick a workspace folder. The agent can list, read, write and edit files there, and edits show a diff preview. It can also run shell commands (output streams into the chat), plan with a todo list, and hand side tasks to short-lived subagents.
  • Shell commands, file writes and file edits pause on an Allow / Deny card unless you turn on "Enable all permissions" in Settings → Agent, which is off by default. I wrote up how that loop works, and where it doesn't protect you, in a separate post.
  • MCP servers can be turned on per chat. It also has skills (type /), persistent memory, token usage by model, and optional web search through TinyFish.
  • Keys stay on your machine. There's no account.

Honest limits:

  • It's a solo project at v1.0.5.
  • The Windows installer is unsigned, so SmartScreen will warn you. macOS is an unsigned beta, and on Linux you build from source.
  • There's no checkpoint or undo. Work in a git repo.
  • There's no Tab autocomplete, and it isn't an editor. I use it next to one.
  • Small local models (I've tested Qwen 3 8B and 27B) do fine on focused edits but get lost on long multi-step tasks. There's no loop guard yet.
  • Anonymous usage telemetry (app opens, feature and model use, token counts; no chats, files, paths or keys) is on by default. You can turn it off in onboarding or Settings → About.

So which one?

  • You want the best editor experience and you're fine paying: Cursor.
  • You want open source with the most features, inside your editor or CLI: Cline.
  • You want a small, standalone open-source app where any OpenAI-compatible or local model drives an agent in a folder, and you approve each command: try OpenPilot, and tell me what breaks.

Links: GitHub · openpilot.in · Run it with Ollama + Qwen 3 · Run it with LM Studio

Disclosure: I drafted this post with help from an AI assistant and checked the claims against each project's docs and source on Oct 17, 2026. If I got something wrong about any of these tools, please correct me in the comments and I'll update it.

articles.title: Building a NoSQL Database in Rust, from Scratch: The Why
articles.description: Series: nosqlite devlog, Part 1  I do this thing sometimes where I get an idea at the wrong time. Not...
articles.body_html:
Series: nosqlite devlog, Part 1

I do this thing sometimes where I get an idea at the wrong time. Not when I have free hours and a clear head, but at 1 AM, mid-week, while I should be doing something else entirely. The idea lands and refuses to leave.

The idea this time was simple on the surface: what if I built a database?

Not a production database. Not the next MongoDB or a distributed cloud thing. Just a small, honest, embedded database. One file, one process, document storage. Something I could actually finish understanding from top to bottom, because I was starting to realize that I had been using databases for years without really knowing what they were doing inside.

That bothered me.

So I started nosqlite. An experiment. A learning project. And what you are reading now is me trying to document how I built it, what I learned, and what it taught me about databases, data structures, systems programming, and Rust itself.

What Are We Actually Building

The description in the README is honest: "trying to build a small embedded nosql database from scratch in rust."

The name is a mashup of two real things: NoSQL and SQLite. Not because it is trying to replace either, but because it takes inspiration from both.

SQLite is one of the most deployed software libraries in human history. Every Android phone has it. Every iOS app probably uses it. Browsers use it. It is a self-contained database that lives in a single file. You do not start a server. You just open a file and start reading and writing. That simplicity is profound when you think about it. The whole database is just a file you can cp, mv, or put on a USB drive.

NoSQL is a broader idea. It basically means "not relational." Instead of tables with fixed columns, you store documents. A document is just a blob of structured data, something like JSON. The shape can vary per record. You do not declare a schema upfront. This model made a lot of sense for applications where data is fluid and hard to predict.

nosqlite tries to marry these two ideas. SQLite-like single file simplicity. NoSQL-like document storage.

That is the goal. And it is entirely an experiment.

Why I Built This in Rust

I was already shifting toward Rust as my primary language. I wrote about that decision separately. But this project cemented it.

Rust is the right tool for something like this because a database engine is fundamentally a systems problem. You are dealing with raw bytes. You are managing a file at the byte level. You are thinking about memory layout, about what happens when a process crashes mid-write, about how data is read back and verified. These are not higher-level concerns.

In TypeScript or Python, you would reach for a library to handle most of this. In Rust, you can actually go down to the level of reading four bytes at a known offset and interpreting them as a little-endian u32. You can describe the exact memory layout of a page. You can write a function that writes bytes into a buffer at a cursor position and have the type system enforce that you do not mess it up.

And the borrow checker, which every newcomer to Rust finds frustrating, becomes genuinely valuable when you are building something like this. You cannot accidentally have two mutable references to the same page buffer. The compiler forces you to think about ownership at every step, which turns out to be exactly what you want when you are building a storage engine.

Understanding What a Database Actually Is

Most developers, including me before this project, have a mental model of a database that looks something like: "you write a query, rows come back." That is the interface. The internals stay hidden.

Here is the simpler version of what actually happens.

A database is ultimately a program that manages a file. The file is structured in a very specific way so that the database can find things quickly, can guarantee that data is not corrupted, and can handle the program crashing at any moment without losing committed data.

Every database, whether it is SQLite or PostgreSQL, has roughly the same set of problems to solve:

How do you organize bytes in the file? You cannot just write raw data one record after another and hope for the best. You need structure. Databases use the concept of a page. A page is a fixed-size chunk of the file, usually 4096 bytes, which matches the OS's memory page size. The database reads and writes entire pages at once.

How do you find records? If every lookup required scanning the entire file, a database with millions of records would be unusably slow. This is where data structures like B-trees come in. B-trees let you find records in logarithmic time. nosqlite does not have a full B-tree index yet, but it is on the roadmap, and I will cover it in a later article.

How do you handle crashes? If you are in the middle of writing when the power goes out, your data should not become corrupt garbage. Most databases solve this with write-ahead logging, abbreviated WAL. You write your intention to a log first, then perform the actual write. On startup, you replay the log. nosqlite plans to implement WAL, but this is also future territory.

How do you support multiple users accessing the same database? This is the concurrency problem. nosqlite currently takes the simple path: only one process can open the database at a time, enforced with a lock file.

The Structure of nosqlite

The project is a Rust workspace with three crates:

nosqlite-core is the storage engine. Everything that reads from and writes to the database file lives here. The pager, the page layout, the catalog (which tracks collections), the document storage logic, the binary codec.

nosqlite-ffi is a C ABI bindings layer. It exposes the core engine through a C-compatible API so that other languages can use it. Go and Python bindings already exist. Dart/Flutter bindings are planned.

nosqlite-shell is a command-line shell. You can open a database file, create collections, insert documents, query them, and delete them, all from the terminal.

That layered design matters. The core does not know or care about what calls it. The FFI layer wraps it in a way that any language with a C FFI can use. The shell is just one consumer among many.

NoSQL Concepts You Need to Know

Before the next articles get into code, it is worth establishing the vocabulary.

Database is the top-level container. In nosqlite, it maps to a single file.

Collection is roughly equivalent to a table in a relational database, but without a fixed schema. In MongoDB, you would call this a collection. In nosqlite, that is the term too.

Document is a single record within a collection. A document is a structured blob of data. nosqlite stores documents in BSON format, which stands for Binary JSON. BSON is what MongoDB uses under the hood. It is like JSON but binary-encoded, which makes it faster to parse and more efficient to store.

ObjectId is a unique identifier automatically assigned to every document. It is a 12-byte value that encodes a timestamp, a machine identifier, and a counter. This is also borrowed from MongoDB.

A typical interaction with nosqlite looks like this through its shell:

create users
insert users { "name": "Priyanshu", "age": 22 }
find users
[
{ "_id": "...", "name": "Priyanshu", "age": 22 }
]

Simple. Intentionally simple. The focus is on understanding what happens under the hood when you type those commands.

The Experiment Mindset

I want to be honest about something. This project is not finished. It probably will not be "finished" in a traditional sense. I am building it as I learn, which means some commits introduce bugs, some commits fix them, and some commits just rename things because I changed my mind about the design. All of that is in the public history.

I am okay with that. This is not a portfolio piece trying to impress someone. It is a record of me figuring things out in public. I find that approach more useful than studying theory alone. When something breaks and I have to debug it at the byte level, I actually understand it. Reading about it in a book does not give me the same thing.

Each article in this series follows the same pattern: a feature lands, I write about it. What the problem was, what I built, what it taught me, what I am still not sure about.

The repository is at https://github.com/PriyanshuPz/nosqlite . The commit history is open. You can see exactly what changed and when.

Now here is the thing that kept me up when I started this project. I had a blank file. A completely empty .nsql file on disk. And I had to decide: what does byte zero mean? What is the very first thing I write? What does the engine look for when it opens that file tomorrow and needs to trust that it is valid?

That question sounds simple. It is not. And the answer to it is the entire next article.

articles.title: Inferred Type Predicates Won't Save filter(Boolean). Here's What Will.
articles.description: TypeScript 5.5 added inferred type predicates, and the internet decided that meant filter(Boolean) finally narrows. It doesn't. Here's exactly what the feature fixed, why the mix-up happened, and the one-line pattern that actually gets you type-safe filtering.
articles.body_html:
Open any "what's new in TypeScript 5.5" roundup from the last two years and you'll find some version of the same line: inferred type predicates finally fixed .filter(Boolean). It gets repeated because it's satisfying — a years-old annoyance, solved for free, no code changes needed. It also isn't true.

The feature that's actually in 5.5 is narrower than the myth, and more useful once you see what it's really for. You've probably been deleting type guards you didn't need to delete, right next to a .filter(Boolean) that's just as untyped as it was in 2019.

The claim, and why it's believable

Here's the example every one of those roundups leads with. Before TypeScript 5.5, this didn't narrow:

const maybeNumbers = [1, null, 2, null, 3];

// previously: (number | null)[] — TypeScript didn't trust the callback
const numbers = maybeNumbers.filter((n) => n !== null);

You wrote a callback that obviously removes null, ran it, and TypeScript still handed you back (number | null)[]. The only way to get a real number[] was to spell it out by hand:

const numbers = maybeNumbers.filter(
  (n): n is number => n !== null
);

That (n): n is number => syntax is a type predicate — a little promise to the compiler that says "if this returns true, treat the input as this narrower type." Writing it by hand, every time, for a check this obvious, was the exact kind of busywork TypeScript is supposed to save you from. TypeScript 5.5 fixed it: the plain (n) => n !== null now gets the predicate inferred automatically. No annotation. Same code, better type.

So far, every word of the popular claim checks out. Here's where it quietly goes off the rails.

Try the one line everyone actually writes

Nobody filters nulls with n !== null in real code nearly as often as they reach for the shorthand:

const configs = [getConfig(), null, getConfig(), undefined];

// still (Config | null | undefined)[] in every TypeScript version as of this writing
const valid = configs.filter(Boolean);

Paste that into the TypeScript playground. The result is still (Config | null | undefined)[] — the exact array you started with, falsy values and all. The feature that rewrote n !== null into a type guard does nothing here, on the single most common one-liner for exactly this job.

Quick gut check before you scroll: what's different between (n) => n !== null and Boolean, if they do the same job?

Why the compiler can see one and not the other

Inferred type predicates work by TypeScript reading a function's body and recognizing a pattern: one return statement, no implicit fall-through, the parameter isn't reassigned, and the thing being returned is a boolean check tied directly to that parameter. (n) => n !== null qualifies on every count — it's a tiny, transparent function, and the compiler can see exactly what it decides and why.

Boolean isn't a function you wrote. It's the global constructor, declared in TypeScript's own standard library as a call signature with no visible implementation — (value?: any) => boolean, full stop. There's no body for the inference engine to read, because as far as the type checker is concerned, there's no body at all. It's an ambient declaration, same category as parseInt or Array.isArray: TypeScript trusts the signature you gave it and nothing more. Teaching the compiler to special-case .filter(Boolean) specifically would mean hard-coding one function name into the type checker — not inference, a workaround with a name attached.

That's the actual boundary of the 5.5 feature: it infers predicates from code it can read. Boolean was never going to be included, in 5.5 or any release after it, unless the standard library itself grows a dedicated overload for it — which, as of this writing, it hasn't.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Why the mix-up happened

Nobody misreported this out of carelessness. .filter(n => n !== null) and .filter(Boolean) solve the identical problem and read, to a human, like two spellings of the same idea. The release notes' headline example uses the first form because it's the clean one to explain in a changelog. Readers who've spent years typing the second form saw "filter now narrows" and reasonably assumed their own habit was covered.

It's the kind of gap that only shows up when you actually run the code, which most roundups — understandably, on a deadline — don't.

What to actually do with your type guards

The real payoff of 5.5 is that you can delete annotations you were writing by hand, as long as the function itself is one TypeScript can read:

// before 5.5 — had to spell out the predicate yourself
function isDefined<T>(value: T): value is NonNullable<T> {
  return value != null;
}

// 5.5+ — this now infers the exact same predicate, with no `is` anywhere
function isDefined<T>(value: T) {
  return value != null;
}

const valid = configs.filter(isDefined); // Config[] — for real this time

That's a genuine win: a helper function you've probably had in a utils.ts file for years just got shorter, and any arrow function shaped like it gets the same treatment for free. What it isn't is a reason to rip out isDefined and go back to .filter(Boolean) for brevity — that one line is exactly where the narrowing still doesn't reach. If you want the one-liner and the types, write the predicate yourself:

const valid = configs.filter(
  (c): c is NonNullable<typeof c> => Boolean(c)
);

Same runtime behavior as .filter(Boolean), three extra words, and an array type you can actually trust downstream.

The takeaway

TypeScript 5.5 didn't make filter(Boolean) type-safe — it made your own boolean-returning functions smart enough that you stop writing is annotations for them by hand. Keep the named helper, drop its predicate syntax, and reach for the explicit inline predicate only when you actually want the Boolean-style one-liner. The compiler was never going to read minds; it just got better at reading your functions.

Next time a changelog claims a one-line fix for a years-old annoyance, paste the actual snippet into the playground before you repeat it. What's one you've seen repeated that didn't hold up?

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.
