Na Starian, a opção foi colocar um servidor Model Context Protocol (MCP) em Python entre o modelo e as bases da empresa:

Camada da Arquitetura Componente / Ambiente Controles de Segurança & Execução Permissão / Escopo
Camada Cliente Modelo de IA / Orquestrador LLM Emite consultas específicas de métricas e contexto sob demanda Ferramentas sob Demanda
├── Camada Lógica Servidor MCP em Python Sanitização de parâmetros, prevenção de SQL injection e limites de consulta Validação & Filtragem
└── Camada Física Banco de Dados Relacional Corporativo Usuário de conexão estritamente restrito a operações SELECT Somente Leitura (Sem Mutações)

Fluxo de segurança em duas camadas com Servidor MCP

A separação opera em dois níveis:

  1. Camada lógica (Servidor MCP): O serviço em Python valida os parâmetros da pergunta, barra tentativas de injeção de SQL e rejeita pedidos excessivamente amplos (como consultas que tentam listar tabelas inteiras sem filtro).
  2. Camada física (Banco de Dados): O usuário de conexão utilizado pelo MCP no banco corporativo tem permissão restrita a SELECT. Não existem concessões de INSERT, UPDATE ou DELETE, o que impede modificações em registros de produção mesmo em caso de erro do modelo.

O servidor também carrega contexto sob demanda: em vez de injetar o esquema completo do banco a cada interação, o MCP disponibiliza apenas as ferramentas necessárias para responder àquela métrica específica. No caso do framework Starian Performance 360, no Projuris Empresa, o sistema unificou consultas cruzando Jira, SonarQube, GitLab e Windsurf, registrando alta de 27,3% na vazão qualificada e taxa de retrabalho de 17,6%.

Red Bull Racing: simulações na OCI

A apresentação de Lucas Leung trouxe o uso de computação de alto desempenho pela Oracle RedBull Racing na Fórmula 1.

Nos finais de semana de corrida, a equipe utiliza clusters com Kubernetes rodando mais de quinhentas CPUs ARM na Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). Em momentos de bandeira amarela ou safety car, o sistema chega a rodar picos de um milhão de simulações de Monte Carlo por segundo, gerando cerca de seis milhões de cenários para avaliar se vale a pena parar nos boxes.

Essa estrutura respaldou a estratégia de Max Verstappen no GP de Miami, quando o piloto largou em nono lugar com pneus duros e estendeu o stint inicial em ar limpo para colocar médios no fim da prova, vencendo a corrida. A decisão no pitwall foi guiada diretamente por esses cálculos de probabilidade em tempo real.

Lovable e Vibe Coding: protótipos rápidos vs. sistemas legados

Alexandre Messina apresentou a trajetória da Lovable e o fluxo de Vibe Coding, mostrando a criação de interfaces funcionais a partir de comandos em linguagem natural.

Entre os exemplos citados, estava o Amosview na Amicci, um sistema de gestão de amostras montado em dois dias por um profissional de operações para resolver um gargalo interno, sem depender de chamados para a equipe de TI. Para validar ideias de produtos, desenhar provas de conceito ou criar ferramentas departamentais simples, a velocidade dessa abordagem é evidente.


Alexandre Messina (Lovable) apresentando a aceleração de protótipos com Vibe Coding.

A fronteira prática aparece quando o protótipo precisa virar produto mantido em escala corporativa. Uma interface montada em linguagem natural resolve a interação inicial, mas não resolve o banco legado com regras acumuladas ao longo de dez anos, filas assíncronas, auditoria ou controle estrito de sessão. Na Lovable é viável estruturar um SaaS com Supabase e Stripe em questão de horas, enquanto nos cenários da Softplan e da 1Doc, o desafio diário é fazer a automação conviver com sistemas legados onde qualquer falha de integridade impacta processos judiciais ou fiscais.

O que fica

Gerar código virou a parte rápida e barata do processo. O trabalho que continua tomando tempo é o de sempre: entender a regra de negócio, desenhar contratos técnicos antes de implementar e garantir testes que segurem regressões.

Saí de lá decidido a estudar mais a fundo o protocolo MCP e escrever especificações melhores antes de pedir código. O resto é conversa.

articles.title: Go error handling patterns that scale: wrapping, unwrapping, sentinels
articles.description: Go's error handling gets a lot of criticism from developers coming from exception-based languages....
articles.body_html:
Go's error handling gets a lot of criticism from developers coming from exception-based languages. But the real problem isn't if err != nil — it's the patterns that get built on top of it. Most tutorials show you bare error returns and call it a day. In a production codebase, you end up with errors that tell you something failed but not where, why, or what caller context led there.

The Problem with Bare Error Returns

Here's the code you write when you're moving fast:

func getUser(id string) (*User, error) {
    row := db.QueryRow("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", id)
    var u User
    if err := row.Scan(&u.ID, &u.Name, &u.Email); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return &u, nil
}

This compiles fine. It even works. But when the error reaches your HTTP handler and you log it, you get:

sql: no rows in result set

That's all. No package name, no function name, no request ID, no context about what was being fetched. Multiply this by 50 functions across 15 packages and you have a log that's useless for debugging.

Wrapping Errors with fmt.Errorf and %w

Go 1.13 introduced the %w verb for fmt.Errorf, which wraps an error while preserving the original for later inspection:

func getUser(id string) (*User, error) {
    row := db.QueryRow("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", id)
    var u User
    if err := row.Scan(&u.ID, &u.Name, &u.Email); err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("getUser(id=%s): %w", id, err)
    }
    return &u, nil
}

Now the error travels up the stack with context attached at each layer:

handler: processRequest: getUser(id=abc123): sql: no rows in result set

The rule I follow: always wrap at the point of origin, never in the middle without adding information. Wrapping fmt.Errorf("getUser: %w", err) inside a loop that calls getUser ten times just adds noise.

One subtle gotcha: %w creates a chain. fmt.Errorf("context: %w", fmt.Errorf("inner: %w", originalErr)) gives you three levels. That's fine — errors.Unwrap navigates the chain, and errors.Is/errors.As traverse it automatically.

Sentinel Errors: When to Use Them

A sentinel error is a package-level variable that callers can compare against:

var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")
var ErrUnauthorized = errors.New("unauthorized")

func getUser(id string) (*User, error) {
    row := db.QueryRow("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", id)
    var u User
    if err := row.Scan(&u.ID, &u.Name, &u.Email); err != nil {
        if errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("getUser(id=%s): %w", id, ErrNotFound)
        }
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("getUser(id=%s): %w", id, err)
    }
    return &u, nil
}

The caller can now do:

user, err := getUser(id)
if errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) {
    http.Error(w, "user not found", http.StatusNotFound)
    return
}

This works because errors.Is traverses the entire error chain — even though ErrNotFound is wrapped inside fmt.Errorf, errors.Is finds it.

When to use sentinels: when callers need to make branching decisions based on the error type. Not found, permission denied, rate limited — these are meaningful categories that affect control flow.

When not to: for every internal error. Package io has io.EOF because it's a legitimate signal, not just a failure. Your internal database timeout doesn't need to be a sentinel unless callers genuinely need to handle it differently.

Custom Error Types for Structured Data

Sometimes you need to carry structured data in an error — an HTTP status code, a field name that failed validation, a request ID for correlation. That's where custom error types come in:

type ValidationError struct {
    Field   string
    Message string
}

func (e *ValidationError) Error() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("validation failed on field %q: %s", e.Field, e.Message)
}

func validateEmail(email string) error {
    if !strings.Contains(email, "@") {
        return &ValidationError{Field: "email", Message: "must contain @"}
    }
    return nil
}

The caller uses errors.As to extract the structured data:

err := validateEmail(input)
var ve *ValidationError
if errors.As(err, &ve) {
    respondWithFieldError(w, ve.Field, ve.Message)
}

errors.As also traverses the chain, so if validateEmail's error gets wrapped by an outer function, errors.As still finds it.

The combination of custom types and wrapping lets you do something powerful: an HTTP handler can catch a *ValidationError and return 400, catch ErrNotFound and return 404, and return 500 for everything else — without knowing the internals of the packages it calls.

Unwrapping: errors.Is, errors.As, and the Chain

Here's the mental model that makes all of this click:

  • errors.Is(err, target) — walks the chain calling == at each step. Use for sentinel comparison.
  • errors.As(err, &target) — walks the chain looking for a type match. Use for custom types.
  • errors.Unwrap(err) — returns the next error in the chain. Rarely call this directly. 
// Chain: wrapErr → ErrNotFound
wrapErr := fmt.Errorf("some context: %w", ErrNotFound)

fmt.Println(errors.Is(wrapErr, ErrNotFound))   // true
fmt.Println(wrapErr == ErrNotFound)             // false — never use == on wrapped errors

This is the most common mistake I see in Go codebases: using == to compare errors after wrapping. It always returns false. Always use errors.Is.

One more thing: if you implement a custom error type that wraps another, implement Unwrap() error to make the chain traversable:

type AppError struct {
    Code    int
    Message string
    Err     error
}

func (e *AppError) Error() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("[%d] %s: %v", e.Code, e.Message, e.Err)
}

func (e *AppError) Unwrap() error {
    return e.Err
}

Without Unwrap, errors.Is and errors.As stop at AppError and can't see what's wrapped inside it.

Sanitizing Errors at the API Boundary

For security-hardened applications, consistent error handling isn't just about debuggability — it's about not leaking internal details to API consumers while still giving operators enough context to diagnose issues.

A pattern I've used in production:

type internalError struct {
    Op  string
    Err error
}

func (e *internalError) Error() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("op=%s: %v", e.Op, e.Err)
}

func (e *internalError) Unwrap() error { return e.Err }

// At the HTTP boundary, sanitize before responding
func sanitizeError(err error) string {
    switch {
    case errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound):
        return "resource not found"
    case errors.Is(err, ErrUnauthorized):
        return "unauthorized"
    default:
        log.Printf("internal error: %v", err) // full chain logged internally
        return "internal server error"
    }
}

The internal error carries full context for your logs. The API caller gets a safe, generic message. The operator log has everything needed to trace the failure back to its source.

The Takeaway

Go error handling scales when you follow three rules consistently:

  1. Wrap with context using fmt.Errorf("op: %w", err) at every layer that adds meaningful information.
  2. Use sentinels only for errors that callers genuinely need to branch on — not for every internal failure.
  3. Use custom types when you need structured data alongside the error message, and always implement Unwrap() when your type wraps another error.

The errors.Is and errors.As functions handle chain traversal automatically. Once you internalize that model, Go error handling stops being a boilerplate tax and starts being a precise contract between layers.

I run AYI NEDJIMI Consultants, a cybersecurity consulting firm. We publish free security hardening checklists — PDF and Excel.

articles.title: Producing Became Cheap, Knowing Became Expensive: What Proud Tech Summit 2026 Reveals About the Frontier Between Prototype and Production
articles.description: I followed the online stream of Proud Tech Summit 2026, an event hosted by Starian and Softplan. It...
articles.body_html:
I followed the online stream of Proud Tech Summit 2026, an event hosted by Starian and Softplan. It was roughly eight hours of presentations focused on software engineering, legacy systems, production AI agents, and data architecture.

The event bypassed the superficial AI chatter that dominates the internet. Instead of canned chat demos, the sessions addressed real problems: legacy relational databases, brittle integrations, fiscal constraints, and the work required to run models with actual customers.

The sessions I followed throughout the day:

  • Carla Souza, Guilherme Brasil, and Luis Fausto (Starian and Softplan): opening and enterprise AI maturity.
  • Lucas Leung (Oracle Brazil): Formula 1 simulations with Oracle RedBull Racing.
  • Jean Roloff (Checklist Fácil / Starian): building Orbit with Working Backwards and SDD.
  • Pedro Escobar (Softplan): agent governance and the Softflow framework.
  • Rafael Gomides and Amanda Aragão (1Doc / Softplan): public municipal service via WhatsApp.
  • Diogo Noschang (Starian): corporate data governance and security with MCP servers.
  • Alexandre Messina (Lovable / VibeLabs): fast prototyping and Vibe Coding.

The three-prompt test and the 77% stalled in pilots

In the opening remarks, Carla Souza pointed out a clear mismatch: the speed of tooling development has accelerated drastically, but the time it takes to grasp business logic and validate systems remains thoroughly human.

Guilherme Brasil demonstrated this with a test using the exact same LLM model. He asked for a 32-word opening statement containing the numbers 5, 10, 15, 25, and 50. Given the bare request, the model produced empty corporate buzzwords about milestones and future impact. When he supplied the actual context - the 5th edition of the summit, 10 years at the company, his daughter's 15th birthday, 25 years of marriage, and turning 50 -, the output became direct and humorous. The model was identical. The difference was solely the context provided in the input.

Luis Fausto presented market research from Gartner and McKinsey on adoption: roughly 77% of companies remain trapped in early pilots and proofs of concept, while only 23% have managed to deploy agentic systems into actual production.

The reason for this bottleneck is operational. For an agent to run in actual production, it requires an accountable owner, explicit Service Level Agreements (SLAs), and a dependable rollback mechanism to recover from errors.

Orbit: three weeks, PR/FAQ, and SDD

Jean Roloff detailed the development of Orbit, Starian's agent platform, built during an intensive three-week sprint.

Before writing code, the team applied Amazon's Working Backwards approach: they wrote the launch press release and internal FAQs (PR/FAQ) as if the product were already finished. The goal was to align customer needs and expected business outcomes before opening the editor.


Jean Muller Roloff (Starian) detailing the Working Backwards approach and PR/FAQ in Orbit.

For development with agents, the team enforced Specification-Driven Development (SDD). Instead of open-ended prompts, they defined data contracts, interfaces, and unit tests before prompting the AI to generate code. The project totaled over 200,000 lines of code with automated test coverage exceeding 90%.

The team also avoided attempting to deploy all fifteen microservices from the planned architecture at once. They isolated a single vertical slice within the Contato Seguro product, focusing purely on report triage, deployed that piece to production to gather live data, and only then expanded to other modules.

Softflow: 220 engineers and four manual gates

At Softplan, the challenge was not a lack of AI adoption, but the uncontrolled spread of custom scripts and prompts across more than 220 engineers, making collaborative codebase maintenance difficult.

Pedro Escobar introduced Softflow, a framework based on the Orchestrator-Workers pattern with eleven distinct stages. The core of the pipeline is its mandatory checkpoints (gates), where execution pauses until a developer validates what was generated.


Pedro Escobar (Softplan) presenting contextual subagent specialization starting from code review.

Stage / Gate Agent Automation / Worker Action Human Validation (Checkpoint) Status / Role
Gate 1 Ingests work item and writes formal technical specification (SDD) Manual approval of SDD before any code is written Specification
├── Worker Generates implementation and runs initial automated suites — Execution
Gate 2 Subagents inspect diff for security, performance & architecture Developer evaluates findings and decides on fixes Review Findings
Gate 3 Creates branch and executes automated integration tests Manual approval required to merge into main Merge Request
Gate 4 Prepares closure and verifies business criteria Human verifies resolution of the business demand Closure

Development pipeline and human validation checkpoints in Softflow

The pipeline organizes validation across four primary stages:

  1. Gate 1 (Specification): The agent reads the work item and writes the formal technical specification (SDD). No code is written before this specification is approved.
  2. Gate 2 (Review Findings): Dedicated subagents scan the diff for security flaws, performance regressions, and architectural inconsistencies. The developer reviews each finding and decides what to fix or dismiss.
  3. Gate 3 (Merge Request): The agent creates the branch and runs the test suite, but merging into the main repository remains a manual approval.
  4. Gate 4 (Closure): A human verifies whether the business demand was actually resolved before closing the work item.

In the live demo, Escobar showed a bug fix in a legacy integration with IBM Jazz RTC, where the API returned empty owner fields. The agent used MCP protocol calls to inspect work items and implemented the patch. Before opening the MR, a review subagent flagged that a logging line lacked an associated unit test. The adjustment was made on the spot, and the merge proceeded with all tests passing.

1Doc: public services on WhatsApp and operational controls

The presentation by Rafael Gomides and Amanda Aragão addressed municipal service delivery via WhatsApp through 1Doc (cases LIA in Limeira and TIA in Florianópolis).

Placing public services on WhatsApp takes advantage of the application's ubiquity, but introduces concrete architectural constraints:


Rafael Gomides (1Doc) explaining the read-contract architecture connecting AI to legacy backends.

In casual chat, people send fragmented messages, voice notes, and change subjects, which does not map cleanly to administrative workflows. The solution involved embedding structured forms within the conversation and programming the agent to route complex edge cases directly to in-person service desks.

Another factor is security: a phone number does not constitute legal identity. For issuing official certificates or reviewing tax debts, 1Doc decoupled authentication: the citizen clicks a temporary link to log into the official web platform, preventing passwords or personal data from circulating in chat history.

Additionally, municipal case creation does not depend on the uptime of a third-party messaging app. Records are saved transactionally to the central database before any notification is dispatched to the user.

For budget and risk control, municipal administrators have toggles to disable specific services on demand, paired with automated alerts at 50%, 70%, 90%, and 100% of contracted quota. If the cap is reached, AI processing shuts down cleanly and requests return to standard support queues.

MCP Server: connecting AI to databases without write permissions

Diogo Noschang addressed how to allow AI models to query enterprise databases without exposing sensitive records or risking accidental mutations.

Legacy databases carry decades of implicit rules and abbreviated table names that language models misinterpret when exposed to raw schemas.

At Starian, the decision was to place a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server written in Python between the model and company databases:

Architecture Layer Component / Environment Security Controls & Enforcement Permission / Scope
Client Layer AI Model / LLM Orchestrator Issues context-specific data and metric queries On-Demand Tools
├── Logical Tier Python MCP Server Parameter sanitization, SQL injection prevention & query limits Validation & Filtering
└── Physical Tier Enterprise Relational Database Database user strictly restricted to SELECT operations Read-Only (No Mutations)

Two-layer security flow via Python MCP Server

Security operates across two distinct tiers:

  1. Logical tier (MCP Server): The Python microservice sanitizes incoming parameters, blocks SQL injection attempts, and rejects overly broad queries (such as prompts trying to dump entire tables without filters).
  2. Physical tier (Database): The database connection user utilized by the MCP server is strictly limited to SELECT. There are no INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE grants, preventing data mutations even in the event of model errors.

The server also manages context on demand: rather than loading entire database schemas on every prompt, the MCP layer provides only the specific tools needed to answer that particular metric. Inside the Starian Performance 360 framework at Projuris Empresa, the setup unified queries across Jira, SonarQube, GitLab, and Windsurf, logging a 27.3% increase in qualified delivery throughput and a 17.6% rework rate.

Red Bull Racing: OCI simulations

Lucas Leung's presentation covered high-performance cloud computing used by Oracle RedBull Racing in Formula 1.

During race weekends, the team provisions Kubernetes clusters running more than 500 ARM CPUs on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). When a yellow flag or safety car alters race conditions, the system runs peaks of one million Monte Carlo simulations per second, evaluating roughly six million scenarios to determine pit stop viability.

This setup backed Max Verstappen's drive at the Miami GP, where he started from ninth on hard tires, stretched his initial stint in clean air, switched to mediums late in the race, and took the victory. The pit wall call was guided directly by these real-time probability simulations.

Lovable and Vibe Coding: rapid prototypes vs. legacy systems

Alexandre Messina discussed the growth of Lovable and the Vibe Coding approach, illustrating the generation of functional interfaces from natural language prompts.

Among the examples shared was Amosview at Amicci, a sample management tool built in two days by an operations specialist to solve an internal bottleneck without submitting tickets to central IT. For validating product concepts, creating proofs of concept, or assembling simple departmental tools, the speed of this workflow is evident.


Alexandre Messina (Lovable) presenting prototype acceleration with Vibe Coding.

The practical boundary appears when a prototype must turn into software maintained at enterprise scale. A prompt-generated interface handles initial interaction, but it does not resolve legacy databases carrying a decade of implicit business rules, asynchronous queues, auditing, or strict session control. In Lovable you can spin up a SaaS with Supabase and Stripe in an afternoon, while in scenarios like Softplan and 1Doc, the daily engineering challenge is making automation live alongside legacy systems where data corruption risks legal and tax compliance.

What remains

Generating code has become the fast and cheap part of the process. The work that continues to demand time is what it has always been: understanding business rules, drafting technical contracts before implementing, and writing tests that catch regressions.

I left the summit determined to study the MCP protocol in depth and write better specifications before asking for code. The rest is just talk.

articles.title: Your First Claude Code Mod: Block Edits Outside the Task's Worktree in 30 Lines
articles.description: Claude Code mods run your JavaScript on every tool call. Build a 30-line mod that refuses Edit and Write outside the task's worktree, then test it.
articles.body_html:
• Book: TypeScript Essentials
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Your agent is working in a git worktree, on its own branch, in a folder next to your main checkout. Then a stack trace from your dev server lands in its context. Every path in that trace points at the main checkout, one directory over. The agent opens ../app/src/config.ts, fixes the bug there, and your "isolated" task has just edited the copy you were using.

Worktrees keep agents apart on disk. They don't stop an agent from writing to a path outside its own folder. In Claude Code's acceptEdits mode, edits outside the working directory still ask you first, but bypassPermissions skips the prompts, and a prompt you approve at the end of a long day is still an approval.

Claude Code v2.1.287 and later can run mods: plugins whose JavaScript or TypeScript handlers run inside Claude Code when an event fires, such as a tool call. A handler can watch the event, change it, or answer it in Claude Code's place. This post builds one that answers Edit and Write calls aimed outside the session's folder with a refusal. It is 30 lines of JavaScript, plus two small JSON files.

What a mod is

A mod is a plugin with three files, laid out the way the create-a-mod tutorial lays out its own:

worktree-guard/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json
└── hooks/
    ├── hooks.json
    └── register.js

plugin.json is the plugin manifest. hooks.json points to your code, and its modules key is what makes the plugin a mod. register.js is the code, which the docs call the hooks module. You don't need Node.js or a build step, because Claude Code loads .js and .ts files directly.

When the mod loads, Claude Code calls the register function the file exports and passes it a function named on. Each on call registers a hook for one event. Every hook gets three arguments: $ (the mods API), e (the event, frozen), and next (the rest of the chain, ending in Claude Code's own behaviour). Return next(e) and the tool runs. Return something else without calling next, and you have answered the event yourself.


The worktree is the plot. The mod is the gate.

Write the guard

Create the directories:

mkdir -p worktree-guard/.claude-plugin \
  worktree-guard/hooks worktree-guard/tests

Save the manifest as worktree-guard/.claude-plugin/plugin.json. Don't start the name with claude-: claude plugin validate fails names that look like Anthropic's own.

{
  "name": "worktree-guard",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "Refuses Edit and Write outside the session root"
}

Save the pointer to your code as worktree-guard/hooks/hooks.json. The path is relative to this file:

{
  "description": "worktree-guard hooks module",
  "modules": ["./register.js"]
}

And the guard itself, worktree-guard/hooks/register.js:

// Refuse Edit/Write outside the session's project root
function normalize(p) {
  const out = []
  for (const part of p.split('/')) {
    if (part === '..') out.pop()
    else if (part && part !== '.') out.push(part)
  }
  return '/' + out.join('/')
}

function isInside(root, file) {
  const r = normalize(root)
  const f = normalize(file.startsWith('/') ? file : r + '/' + file)
  return f === r || f.startsWith(r + '/')
}

async function guard($, e, next) {
  const root = await $.session.root()
  if (isInside(root, e.file_path)) return next(e)
  return { deny: `${e.file_path} is outside ${root}. ` +
    'Edit files in this worktree, or ask the user first.' }
}

export function register(on) {
  on('tool.call', { tool: ['Edit', 'Write'] }, guard)
    .catch(async ($, e, next) => {
      if (next.called) return next(e)
      return { deny: 'worktree-guard failed: ' + next.error.kind }
    })
}

{ tool: ['Edit', 'Write'] } is the matcher, a filter. An array matches any value in it, so the hook runs for those two tools only. Both carry their target as e.file_path, the field the events guide reads in its own Edit/Write example.

For the root, the mods API has both $.session.cwd() and $.session.root(). The type declarations describe root() as where the session started, or where /cd or a worktree move took it, and say a shell cd during the session does not move it. That is the boundary you want: start Claude Code in a worktree and the root is that worktree.

The hooks module has no Node.js APIs, so there is no path module to lean on (API docs). normalize folds ., .. and doubled slashes by hand, so /work/app/../main/x.ts becomes /work/main/x.ts before the comparison. The r + '/' in the prefix test stops /work/app-old from passing as a child of /work/app.

Returning { deny } without calling next means the tool never runs and no permission prompt appears. Claude reads the deny text as the tool's result, so write it as an instruction. Claude Code runs its permission check inside next, so the refusal holds in every permission mode, bypassPermissions included.

A hook that throws or times out is skipped, and the edit would go through. The .catch handler makes the guard fail closed: if guard failed before calling next, the edit is refused. The handler has a one-second limit of its own (reference), and if it fails too, the hook is skipped.

Load it and check what it touches

Load the directory for one session, without installing anything:

claude --plugin-dir ./worktree-guard

Type /plugin at the prompt. The overview says a dim line under the tabs gives the count and the names of loaded mods, so this one should read 1 mod active · worktree-guard. If the name is missing, the module didn't load.

Ask Claude to change a file one level up, for example add a comment to the top of ../README.md. The call should come back refused, with your message as the result. An edit inside the folder goes through as usual. Claude Code hot-reloads a --plugin-dir mod when you save a file in it, so you can tweak the deny text without restarting.

Before you share a mod, or install someone else's, read it the way Claude Code does:

claude plugin validate ./worktree-guard

validate runs the same static analysis Claude Code runs at load time, without executing your code. Look at three lines. The hooks: line should list tool.call with its tool filter in braces. The calls: line should list $.session.root and nothing else: no $.fs, no $.process, no $.http. And because this hook can refuse an action, validate prints a gating-hook line saying whether it has a .catch handler. This one does.

That calls: line is your audit. Mods aren't sandboxed: they run with your permissions and can read files, start processes and make network requests through the mods API.

Test it without a session

claude plugin test runs any *.test.ts file in the plugin directory with no session, sign-in or network (test docs). Nothing real answers in a test, so you stub the session root and the tool itself. Save this as worktree-guard/tests/guard.test.ts:

import { expect, test } from 'claude-code/testing'

test('refuses a write outside the root', async ($, on) => {
  on('session.root', () => ({ value: '/work/app' }))
  on('tool.call', () => ({ result: 'ok' }))
  const out = await $.tool.call({
    tool: 'Write',
    file_path: '/work/app/../main/x.ts',
    content: '',
  })
  expect(out.deny).toBeDefined()
})

test('lets an edit inside the root through', async ($, on) => {
  on('session.root', () => ({ value: '/work/app' }))
  on('tool.call', () => ({ result: 'ok' }))
  const out = await $.tool.call({
    tool: 'Edit',
    file_path: '/work/app/src/a.ts',
    old_string: 'a',
    new_string: 'b',
  })
  expect(out).toEqual({ result: 'ok' })
})

A stub for a mods API call is named without the $. and returns { value }. The tool.call stub stands in for Claude Code running the tool, so a call the guard lets through resolves to { result: 'ok' }. Run claude plugin test from the worktree-guard directory; it exits with status 1 on a failure, so it fits in CI. I haven't run this suite myself, so if a field name disagrees with your build, trust the declarations Claude Code writes into .claude-plugin/types/.

Every Hermes task, guarded

The guard gets more useful when every task already has a worktree. I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. In Hermes, ⌘N (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux) starts each task on its own hermes/<name> branch, in its own worktree, with the task as the agent's first prompt. Claude Code runs there as the regular CLI in a real terminal, so a Claude Code session in a Hermes task starts with its root at that task's worktree.


The ⌘N New task sheet in Hermes 2.3.4: Claude Code, the orders-api project, a new hermes/ worktree, Accept edits, and a preview of the claude command Hermes will run.

You can't add --plugin-dir to a command you don't type yourself. For that case Claude Code reads CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS, an environment variable the reference describes as plugin directories "for apps you can't pass a flag to". It takes absolute paths and can live in the env block of ~/.claude/settings.json:

{
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS": "/path/to/mods/worktree-guard"
  }
}

Put the mod somewhere outside your repositories, so no task can rewrite the guard through Edit or Write. From then on, every normal Claude Code session loads the mod, wherever it was started, and an Edit or Write aimed outside the folder Hermes made for the task comes back refused.


The Review Desk's Worktrees tab: one Hermes worktree each for orders-api, web-app and orders-types, with each one's hermes/ branch, task, age and disk size.

One interaction to know about. Since Hermes 2.3.0, a task can include up to 5 extra folders, and those are worked on where they are, on their current branch, not in the task's worktree. The guard will refuse Claude's edits in them. If you use extra folders, add their paths to an allow list in isInside, or leave the guard off for those tasks.

What this mod doesn't stop

It guards two tools by path. It is not a sandbox.

  • Bash. sed -i, cp or echo > into ../app never goes through Edit or Write. Outside bypassPermissions, Claude Code checks output redirects and tee targets against the working directories and asks first. Its sandboxing isolates the Bash commands Claude runs.
  • Other writers. NotebookEdit and MCP tools that write files carry their paths in other fields. Add them to the matcher with the field each one uses.
  • Symlinks. The check compares path strings. A symlink inside the worktree that points outside it passes.
  • Subagents. tool.call fires for subagent calls too. I haven't checked what $.session.root() returns inside a subagent that runs in its own worktree, so test that before you rely on it.
  • POSIX paths only. normalize splits on /. On Windows you would need to handle drive letters and backslashes.

If you'd rather not write JavaScript, a PreToolUse settings hook running a script you already have can block the same calls, and the docs' comparison table recommends exactly that case for settings hooks. What the mod adds is claude plugin test and a validate report anyone can read before loading it.

If this was useful

The hooks module is a plain ES module of async functions, and once you rename it to register.ts and point modules at the new name, the declarations Claude Code writes into .claude-plugin/types/ narrow e as soon as you check e.tool. That is the everyday TypeScript in TypeScript Essentials: types, narrowing, modules and async, across Node, Bun, Deno and the browser. If you write mods, it's the book that makes those type files read like documentation.

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

Start with books 1 and 2. Coming from Kotlin or Java, take book 3 in place of book 1; coming from PHP, book 4. If you ship TypeScript at work, add book 5.

Hermes IDE is free, source-available under BSL 1.1, on macOS, Windows and Linux, and not affiliated with Anthropic or any agent vendor: download it or star it on GitHub.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: Claude Code Context Window Management in 2026: What Gets Included, What Gets Dropped, and How to Control It
articles.description: Most Claude Code performance problems stem from unmanaged context windows. Learn what gets included, what gets dropped, and how to control the auto-compaction process that silently deletes your conversation history.
articles.body_html:
Claude Code Context Window Management in 2026: What Gets Included, What Gets Dropped, and How to Control It

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Most Claude Code performance problems stem from developers treating the context window as infinite. The agent stops responding to recent changes, forgets path rules you just defined, or produces code that ignores constraints you set three messages ago. Teams assume the model degraded or the service is slow. The actual cause is simpler: the context window reached capacity and auto-compacted, silently dropping the information you needed most.

The context window is a fixed-size buffer. Claude Code's 200k token limit holds your conversation, active files, skill invocations, and path rules. When that buffer fills, the agent discards content according to a priority hierarchy. Path rules vanish before conversation history. Conversation history vanishes before file content. The skill listing never reloads. Understanding this hierarchy changes how you structure long sessions.

This post covers the auto-compaction process, the drop hierarchy, manual control commands, subagent isolation, and production patterns that keep critical context available. Apply these techniques and your Claude Code sessions will stay coherent across thousands of messages.

Key Takeaways

  • Claude Code's 200k token context window holds conversation, files, skills, and path rules, and auto-compacts when full by silently dropping content in a fixed priority order.
  • Path rules and conversation history are the first to be discarded during auto-compaction, while active file content and invoked skills persist longest.
  • The /compact command manually triggers compaction on your terms, and the /clear command wipes all conversation history to reclaim maximum context space.
  • Subagents run with isolated context windows, preventing parent session clutter from degrading delegated task performance.
  • Strategic context management means explicitly preserving critical constraints (path rules, design decisions) in file artifacts rather than relying on conversation history.

What Gets Included in Claude Code's Context Window

The context window is a ranked collection of content types. Not everything you say or every file you open consumes space equally. Claude Code loads content in this order:

System prompt and core instructions occupy the top of the window. These never get dropped. The agent's identity, capabilities, and base constraints live here. This is why the agent always knows it can run shell commands or invoke skills, regardless of how full the context becomes.

Active file content loads next. When you open a file or the agent reads one, the full text enters the window. Large files consume proportional space. A 50k line TypeScript definition file takes more tokens than a 200-line React component. The agent keeps recently accessed files in memory until it needs the space for something else.

Invoked skill content follows. Each skill you run adds its implementation to the context. The skill listing (the index of available skills) remains static and never reloads, but the actual code for skills you invoke does enter the window. This matters because repeatedly invoking different skills churns the context. A session that calls 15 unique skills carries more overhead than one that calls 3 skills 15 times.

Path rules come next. These are the constraints you define with commands like "never touch files in /vendor" or "use single quotes in all TypeScript files." Path rules are metadata, not code. They consume fewer tokens than file content but more than you expect. A project with 30 path rules can occupy 5,000 tokens.

Conversation history fills the remaining space. This is every message you sent and every response the agent produced. Long conversations with code examples, error traces, and multi-turn debugging consume the bulk of the context window. A 50-message exchange can easily reach 80k tokens.

Claude Code context window composition showing the layered priority of content types

The implication here is that conversation history is the most expendable. When the window fills, the agent sacrifices old messages before it drops file content or skills. This is why long debugging sessions feel like the agent forgot your earlier decisions. It did not forget. The context window deleted those messages.

The Auto-Compaction Process: When Context Reaches Its Limit

Auto-compaction is the background process that prevents the context window from overflowing. When token count approaches 200k, the agent triggers compaction automatically. This happens silently. No warning, no confirmation. The agent just removes content and continues.

The trigger threshold sits around 190k tokens. The agent does not wait until 200k because processing the next message would exceed capacity. It compacts preemptively to maintain headroom. The exact threshold varies slightly based on internal heuristics, but 190k is the practical floor.

Compaction follows a strict order. The agent drops conversation history first, starting with the oldest messages. It removes entire exchanges, not individual messages. If a three-message debugging thread exists at the start of your session, compaction deletes all three messages as a unit.

After conversation history, the agent discards path rules. It prioritizes recently used rules over old ones. A path rule you defined 100 messages ago that the agent has not referenced since will vanish before a rule you set 10 messages ago that guided recent decisions.

File content and invoked skills are the last to be removed. The agent assumes you need the code you are actively working with more than you need historical context. This assumption holds in most cases, but it creates a failure mode: if you are debugging an issue that stems from a decision made 50 messages ago, and compaction has already dropped that context, the agent cannot recover the reasoning.

The auto-compaction process is deterministic. Two sessions that reach 190k tokens with identical content will compact in the same order. This predictability is useful. Once you understand the hierarchy, you can structure your workflow to keep critical information in the retained portion.

What Gets Dropped First: Skills, Path Rules, and Conversation History

The drop hierarchy is simple but counterintuitive. Developers assume the agent prioritizes recently defined constraints. It does not. Recency applies only within a content category, not across categories.

Conversation history drops first. The agent removes the oldest messages in your session. If you had a 20-message exchange debugging a TypeScript error, then switched to implementing a new feature, and the context window filled, the entire debugging exchange vanishes. The agent retains the feature implementation messages because they are more recent.

Path rules drop second. The agent removes rules it has not applied recently. If you defined a rule that "all API routes must include rate limiting middleware" but have not created an API route in the last 50 messages, that rule is a compaction target. The agent tracks rule usage internally. A rule that guided decisions in the last 10 messages persists longer than one that has not been referenced in 100 messages.

Skill invocations drop third. The agent removes the implementation code for skills you invoked early in the session. The skill listing (the index of available skills) never gets dropped, so the agent still knows the skill exists. But the actual code for how the skill works is no longer in context. This matters if you ask the agent to modify or debug a skill. Without the implementation in context, the agent must re-invoke the skill to see its code.

Active file content drops last. The agent removes files you have not accessed recently. If you opened a file 100 messages ago, made changes, then switched to working on other files, the original file becomes a compaction target. The agent assumes you finished working with it. If you return to that file later, the agent must reload it, which consumes tokens again.

The failure mode here is silent degradation. The agent does not tell you it dropped your path rules. It just stops applying them. A team that defines strict formatting rules at the start of a session, then works through 200 messages of implementation, will find the agent producing code that violates those rules. The rules are gone. The only fix is to redefine them, which consumes context space again.

This distinction is critical. Teams treat conversation history as durable state. It is not. Anything you need the agent to remember must live in a file or a path rule. If a design decision matters, write it into a decisions.md file. If a constraint matters, define it as a path rule and re-invoke it periodically to keep it recent.

Manual Control: Using /compact and /clear Commands

The agent provides two commands for manual context management. These commands override the auto-compaction process and give you control over what stays and what goes.

The /compact command triggers compaction immediately. Instead of waiting for the context window to reach 190k tokens, you force compaction on your terms. This is useful when you finish a debugging session and want to clear that context before starting a new feature. The command follows the same drop hierarchy as auto-compaction: conversation history first, then path rules, then skills, then files.

// After a long debugging session
// Run: /compact

// Before compaction: 185k tokens
// After compaction: 120k tokens
// Old debugging exchanges removed
// Path rules and active files preserved

The /clear command is more aggressive. It wipes all conversation history but preserves everything else. Path rules, active files, and invoked skills remain in context. This is the nuclear option. Use it when conversation history has become noise and you want a fresh start without reloading your entire workspace.

// After 500 messages of implementation
// Run: /clear

// Before clear: 195k tokens
// After clear: 85k tokens
// All conversation history removed
// Path rules, files, skills intact

The difference between /compact and /clear matters. Compact removes the oldest content gradually, preserving recent exchanges. Clear removes all conversation history immediately, regardless of recency. Use compact when you want to trim the context but keep recent decisions. Use clear when you want maximum space and can afford to lose all conversational context.

Manual compaction is a production pattern. Teams that run long Claude Code sessions (8+ hours, 1000+ messages) schedule compaction breaks. Every 200 messages, the lead developer runs /compact to prevent auto-compaction from triggering at an inconvenient moment. This keeps the context window under control and ensures critical decisions remain in memory.

The other production pattern is preemptive clearing. Before starting a high-stakes task (like a production deployment or a major refactor), run /clear to maximize available context. This ensures the agent has full capacity for the task ahead. The cost is losing conversation history. The benefit is predictable performance.

Subagent Context Isolation: Fresh Windows for Delegated Tasks

Subagents are the escape hatch for context window constraints. When you delegate a task to a subagent, Claude Code spawns a new agent instance with a fresh 200k token context window. The subagent inherits no conversation history from the parent session. It starts clean.

This matters for long-running workflows. A parent agent that has consumed 180k tokens of context can delegate a task to a subagent, and that subagent has the full 200k token budget. The parent's context does not pollute the subagent's window. The subagent also cannot see the parent's conversation history, which prevents it from being confused by unrelated decisions.

The isolation is bidirectional. The subagent cannot access the parent's context, and the parent cannot see the subagent's internal conversation. When the subagent completes, it returns a result to the parent. That result enters the parent's context window as a single artifact. If the subagent produced 50 messages of internal debugging, the parent only sees the final output.

This pattern is essential for complex workflows. A parent agent coordinating a multi-file refactor can delegate each file to a separate subagent. Each subagent works in isolation with full context capacity. The parent receives the completed changes and merges them. The parent's context window only grows by the size of the final diffs, not by the size of the subagents' internal conversations.

The failure mode is over-delegation. Spawning a subagent has overhead. The subagent must reload files it needs, re-invoke skills, and reconstruct understanding. If the task is small (a 10-line function), delegation costs more than it saves. If the task is large (a 500-line module), delegation is a net win. The breakeven point is around 100 lines of code or 10 messages of conversation.

Related: Claude Code Memory Strategies in 2026 covers how to structure durable context that survives compaction cycles, and Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf in Production 2026 compares subagent patterns across tools.

Strategic Context Management: Keeping What Matters

Strategic context management is about making explicit what the auto-compaction process treats as implicit. The agent assumes old conversation history is expendable. You must override that assumption by encoding critical information in durable artifacts.

The first pattern is the decision log. Create a docs/decisions.md file at the start of the project. Every time you make a significant architectural decision, add an entry. Include the decision, the reasoning, and the date. When the agent needs context for why the codebase is structured a certain way, point it to the decision log. This file lives in the context window as active content, not as conversation history, so it persists through compaction.

// docs/decisions.md
// Decision Log

// 2026-10-15: Use Zod for all API validation
// Reasoning: Runtime validation catches client errors before they hit the database.
// Standardizes error messages across endpoints. Zod schemas double as TypeScript types.
// Alternative considered: Joi (more verbose, no TypeScript inference).

// 2026-10-14: Colocate tests with implementation files
// Reasoning: Reduces friction for test updates during refactors.
// Makes it obvious when a module lacks tests.
// Alternative considered: /tests directory (harder to maintain parity with /src).

The second pattern is active path rule management. Do not define path rules once and forget them. Revisit rules every 50 messages. If a rule still matters, mention it explicitly so the agent re-applies it and refreshes its usage timestamp. If a rule no longer matters, remove it. Stale path rules consume context and degrade performance.

Strategic context management showing decision logs and path rule refresh cycles

The third pattern is periodic file pruning. Close files you are not actively working on. The agent keeps open files in context even if you have not touched them in 100 messages. If you opened 10 files during a debugging session, then switched to a new feature, close the debugging files. The agent will drop them from context, reclaiming space for the feature work.

The fourth pattern is subagent delegation for disposable work. If you need to explore an implementation approach but are not sure it will work, delegate it to a subagent. The subagent can consume its full context window experimenting. If the approach fails, the parent's context is unaffected. If the approach succeeds, the parent imports the final code. This keeps the parent's context clean and focused.

Strategic context management is a discipline. It requires awareness of what is in context and what matters. Teams that adopt these patterns report 30% fewer context-related failures and 40% longer effective session durations. The cost is the overhead of maintaining decision logs and pruning files. The benefit is predictable agent behavior across long workflows.

Context Window vs Token Budget: Understanding the Real Cost

The context window and the token budget are separate concepts. The context window is the 200k token limit on what the agent can hold in memory. The token budget is the monthly or session-based cap on how many tokens you can generate. Confusing the two leads to poor cost management.

Every message you send and every response the agent generates consumes token budget. Reading a file also consumes budget because the agent must tokenize the content. Invoking a skill consumes budget because the skill implementation enters context. The budget is cumulative. A 1000-message session that generates 500k tokens of responses depletes budget faster than a 100-message session that generates 50k tokens.

The failure mode is treating the context window as the primary cost control. Developers compact aggressively to keep context below 100k tokens, assuming this saves budget. It does not. Compaction removes content from the window but does not refund token budget. Once tokens are spent reading files or generating responses, they are gone.

The real cost control is reducing token generation. Shorter responses consume less budget. Fewer file reads consume less budget. Delegating to subagents does not save budget because the subagent's token usage still counts toward your total. The only way to reduce budget consumption is to generate less content.

This distinction is critical. A session that uses 180k tokens of context window but generates 50k tokens of responses is cheaper than a session that uses 80k tokens of context window but generates 200k tokens of responses. Context window size correlates with budget usage but does not determine it. Output volume determines it.

The practical implication is that you should optimize for output efficiency, not context minimization. Use /compact to keep the context window manageable and the agent responsive. But if your goal is cost reduction, focus on reducing response length and file access frequency. Ask the agent for concise answers. Batch file reads instead of opening files incrementally.

Related: Claude Code Git Diffs, Hunks, and Commit Decisions covers how to structure Git workflows that minimize redundant file reads and reduce token budget consumption during code review.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if the agent runs out of context during a response?

The agent truncates the response mid-generation and returns what it has produced so far. The context window does not expand to accommodate the completion. Subsequent messages continue from the truncated state. The lost content is unrecoverable unless you regenerate the response after compacting.

Can I increase the 200k token context window limit?

No. The 200k limit is a hard constraint of the Claude Code architecture as of 2026. Anthropic has not announced plans to increase it. The only workaround is delegation to subagents, which provide independent 200k token windows.

Do path rules persist across sessions?

No. Path rules live in the context window, not in durable storage. When you close Claude Code, all path rules are lost. To preserve them, write them into a path-rules.md file and re-apply them at the start of each session by asking the agent to read and enforce the file.

How can I see my current context window usage?

Claude Code does not expose a built-in token counter. The best approximation is to track message count and file size manually. A rough heuristic: each message with a short response consumes 500-1000 tokens. A 10k line file consumes 15k-20k tokens. These are estimates; actual token counts vary.

Does compaction affect subagent memory?

No. Subagents have isolated context windows. Parent compaction does not affect subagent context, and subagent compaction does not affect parent context. When a subagent returns a result, only the final output enters the parent's context, not the subagent's internal conversation.

Production Patterns: Context Management at Scale

Production-grade Claude Code workflows treat context as a managed resource. Teams that run multi-day sessions with thousands of messages adopt patterns that prevent silent degradation and keep the agent effective.

The first pattern is scheduled compaction. Every 200 messages, the lead developer runs /compact. This prevents auto-compaction from triggering during critical work. Scheduled compaction happens during natural breaks (lunch, end of day, between features). The team knows context is clean before starting the next task.

The second pattern is role-based delegation. Large features split into subagent tasks. One subagent handles API routes. Another handles UI components. A third handles database migrations. Each subagent works in isolation with full context capacity. The parent coordinates integration. This keeps the parent's context window focused on high-level coordination instead of implementation details.

The third pattern is decision artifact enforcement. Every architectural decision, every constraint, every design choice gets written into a docs/ file. The agent references these files instead of relying on conversation history. When compaction drops old messages, the durable artifacts remain. This pattern eliminates the "agent forgot our earlier decision" failure mode.

That covers the essential patterns for Claude Code context window management. Apply these in production and the difference will be immediate: longer sessions without degradation, fewer constraint violations, and predictable agent behavior across thousands of messages. The context window is finite. Treat it as a constraint, not an assumption, and your workflows scale.

articles.title: Why Traditional Sourdough Calculators Have a Hidden 3% Water Error (And How We Fixed It With Rheology & Thermodynamics)

articles.body_html:
If you ask any software engineer what their weekend hobby is, there is a surprisingly high probability the answer is sourdough bread baking.

Both disciplines scratch the same neurological itch: deterministic algorithms meeting complex organic state machines. You feed living wild yeast cultures, balance flour-to-water ratios, and wait for bulk fermentation state transitions.

Yet, after baking hundreds of loaves and analyzing popular bread calculators across the web, I discovered a glaring mathematical flaw that plagues almost every conventional baking calculator: the hidden 3% hydration trap.

Here is why standard calculators fail, the polymer science behind dough stickiness, and how we engineered an open-source, edge-rendered solution using Next.js 14, Cloudflare, and thermodynamic physics.

1. The Hidden 3% Hydration Flaw

In standard baker's percentage accounting, every ingredient is calculated relative to the total flour weight ($100\%$).

A classic recipe might read:

  • Flour: $500\text{g}$ ($100\%$)
  • Water: $375\text{g}$ ($75\%$)
  • Levain (Starter): $100\text{g}$ ($20\%$)
  • Salt: $10\text{g}$ ($2\%$)

The baker assumes they are handling a $75\%$ hydration dough.

The Mathematical Bug:

A standard sourdough starter is maintained at $100\%$ hydration (equal parts flour and water by weight). That means your $100\text{g}$ of levain is secretly:

  • $50\text{g}$ flour
  • $50\text{g}$ water

When you recalculate the True Total Hydration across the entire dough matrix:
$$\text{Total Flour} = 500\text{g} + 50\text{g} = 550\text{g}$$
$$\text{Total Water} = 375\text{g} + 50\text{g} = 425\text{g}$$
$$\text{True Total Hydration} = \frac{425\text{g}}{550\text{g}} \times 100\% = \mathbf{77.27\%}$$

That is a $+2.27\%$ unexpected surge in liquid water! If the baker uses a higher inoculation (e.g. $25\%$ starter), the error spikes beyond $+3.2\%$.

To a baker aiming for a manageable $75\%$ loaf, an unexpected $78\%$ matrix means the gluten network loses its elastic modulus ($G'$), resulting in an uncontrollable, sticky puddle on the bench.

2. Modeling Multi-Flour Water Absorption Limits

Different flours possess radically different water absorptions due to damaged starch, protein content, and pentosan polymers:

  • Unbleached Bread Flour: baseline $72\%\text{ - }76\%$
  • Stoneground Whole Wheat: bran fibers absorb water rapidly ($80\%\text{ - }85\%$)
  • Rye Flour: rich in mucilaginous arabinoxylans, absorbing up to $85\%\text{ - }90\%$ water but forming zero traditional gluten networks.

We modeled this in TypeScript as a weighted absorption rheology engine:

export interface FlourComponent {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  weightGrams: number;
  proteinPercent: number;
  absorptionRatio: number; // e.g. 0.74 for bread flour, 0.85 for rye
}

export function calculateEffectiveAbsorptionCapacity(flours: FlourComponent[]): number {
  const totalWeight = flours.reduce((acc, f) => acc + f.weightGrams, 0);
  if (totalWeight === 0) return 0.75;

  const weightedSum = flours.reduce(
    (acc, f) => acc + f.weightGrams * f.absorptionRatio,
    0
  );
  return weightedSum / totalWeight;
}

3. The Summer DDT Crisis: When Water Must Be Colder Than Ice

Professional bakers rely on Desired Dough Temperature (DDT) to control fermentation kinetics:
$$T_{\text{water}} = (3 \times \text{DDT}) - (T_{\text{room}} + T_{\text{flour}} + T_{\text{starter}} + \text{Friction Factor})$$

The Physical Impossibility in Hot Climates:

Suppose your summer kitchen is at $86^\circ\text{F}$ ($30^\circ\text{C}$), flour is $84^\circ\text{F}$, starter is $82^\circ\text{F}$, and mixer friction is $4^\circ\text{F}$. You target a standard DDT of $76^\circ\text{F}$.

Plug this into the formula:
$$T_{\text{water}} = (3 \times 76) - (86 + 84 + 82 + 4) = 228 - 256 = \mathbf{-28^\circ\text{F}}\;(-33.3^\circ\text{C})$$

Liquid water cannot exist at $-28^\circ\text{F}$.

Standard calculators either crash, throw an error, or tell the baker "chill your water," which is physically inadequate because liquid water cannot drop below $32^\circ\text{F}$ ($0^\circ\text{C}$).

The Thermodynamic Fix: Latent Heat of Fusion

Ice does not merely cool water by its temperature difference—it absorbs $80\text{ cal/g}$ ($334\text{ J/g}$) of energy purely to break hydrogen bonds during phase change (latent heat of fusion).

We implemented the thermodynamic energy balance equation:
$$m_{\text{ice}} = m_{\text{water, total}} \times \frac{T_{\text{tap}} - T_{\text{target}}}{T_{\text{tap}} + 144 - T_{\text{ice}} \times 0.5}$$
(where 144 is the BTU/lb latent heat constant)

With this equation, the engine computes the exact gram-for-gram replacement:

  • Crushed Ice: $142\text{g}$
  • Chilled Tap Water: $233\text{g}$

When the ice melts during autolyse, the resulting bulk dough hits $76^\circ\text{F}$ within $\pm 0.5^\circ\text{F}$.

4. Open-Sourcing the Rheology Engine

We extracted the core mathematics and thermodynamic physics into a zero-dependency open-source library:

  • GitHub Repository: forestelf/sourdough-physics
  • Live Web App: SourdoughCalc.app
  • License: MIT

The frontend is built on Next.js 14 App Router, deployed globally to Cloudflare Pages edge locations with $<50\text{ms}$ Time to First Byte (TTFB). It also includes a kitchen companion mode with the Screen Wake Lock API, keeping your phone display alive while kneading flour-covered dough.

5. What's Next?

We recently added kinetic microbial timing for starter feeding ratios ($1:1:1$, $1:2:2$, $1:5:5$) and geometric bulk rise calibration for conical mixing bowls.

Are you baking sourdough or working on computational food science? Check out the live tool or explore the code on GitHub. Feedback and edge-case pull requests are warmly welcomed!

articles.title: Why Clean 48kHz Voice Clips Look Like 128kbps MP3s to Naive FFTs (And How to Fix It in WebAudio)
articles.description: Imagine you are building an automated audio QA pipeline for a game studio. You want to catch fake...
articles.body_html:
Imagine you are building an automated audio QA pipeline for a game studio. You want to catch fake "lossless" WAV files—assets where someone took a 128 kbps MP3 from a stock site, re-saved it as a 48.0 kHz · 16-bit PCM WAV, and committed it to the repository.

The textbook approach seems obvious: run a Fast-Fourier Transform (FFT) across the audio buffer, average the magnitude spectrum across all frames, and scan downward from the Nyquist frequency (24.0 kHz) until the energy rises above your noise floor threshold (say, -75 dBFS). If the energy dies out below 16.5 kHz, flag it as a 128 kbps MP3 transcode.

It works great on mastered synthwave tracks. Then a voice actor uploads a studio-clean, uncompressed 48.0 kHz · 16-bit PCM dialogue line—and your analyzer immediately flags it as:

❌ High-Frequency Roll-Off Detected — Brickwall cutoff at 2.0 kHz (~128 kbps MP3 transcode)

Wait—why did a pristine 48 kHz voice recording get flagged as a low-bitrate MP3 with a 2.0 kHz cutoff?

Here is the DSP postmortem of why time-averaged linear FFTs fail catastrophically on speech and game sound effects (SFX), and the exact math we used to fix it in pure TypeScript and WebAudio.

1. Why Time-Averaged FFTs Misclassify Human Speech & Game SFX

Mastered music is broadband and dense: cymbals, hi-hats, and stereo reverbs keep high-frequency bins (10–20 kHz) energized across nearly the entire track.

Dialogue and game SFX behave completely differently:

  1. Vowel Energy Is Concentrated Below 3.5 kHz: A male or female voice has a fundamental frequency ($F_0$) between 85 Hz and 300 Hz, and its primary vocal tract resonances (Formants $F_1, F_2, F_3$) sit between 300 Hz and 3,400 Hz. Above 4 kHz, natural glottal roll-off drops at roughly -12 dB/octave.
  2. High-Frequency Consonants Are Sparse Transients: Unvoiced fricatives and sibilance (s, sh, f, t) do contain energy up to 12–18 kHz, but they only last 40–80 ms—less than 6% to 8% of the frames in a spoken phrase.
  3. Temporal Averaging Erases Transient Highs: When you compute the mean dB across all STFT frames, those brief 8 kHz–16 kHz consonant bursts are averaged with 92% of voiced/quiet frames sitting at -95 dBFS. The mean spectrum plunges below your -75 dBFS detection floor right around 2.0–3.5 kHz. 
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│             Natural Voice Roll-off vs. Codec Brickwall Cliff            │
├──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┤
│ Metric                   │ Clean 48kHz Voice    │ 128kbps MP3 Transcode │
├──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤
│ Mean Spectrum > 4 kHz    │ -82 dBFS (Sparse!)   │ -64 dBFS (Music)      │
│ 98th Percentile > 10 kHz │ -48 dBFS (Consonants)│ -98 dBFS (Dead)       │
│ Roll-off Slope           │ ~15–28 dB / octave   │ >= 60 dB / octave     │
│ Cutoff Band              │ Gradual (2–14 kHz)   │ Sharp (15.5–16.5 kHz) │
└──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘

2. Fix #1: 98th-Percentile Peak Envelope ($E_{98}$) + Brickwall Slope ($ ext{dB/octave}$)

To distinguish a genuine lossy codec low-pass filter from natural acoustic roll-off, you need two mathematical invariants:

  1. Use the 98th-Percentile Active-Frame Envelope ($E_{98}$), Not the Mean: First, gate out silent frames (RMS < -60 dBFS). Across the remaining active frames, compute the 98th percentile magnitude in each frequency bin. If a voice clip has even a single crisp "s" or breath transient reaching 17 kHz, $E_{98}$ captures it immediately.
  2. Measure Cliff Steepness ($ ext{dB/octave}$) Inside Codec Cutoff Bands: Lossy encoders (LAME MP3, AAC, Opus) don't roll off gently at 2 kHz. They apply a polyphase filterbank cliff inside specific codec bands (14.5 kHz – 20.5 kHz) with a steepness of $ge 60 ext{ dB/octave}$: 
/**
 * Evaluates whether a candidate cutoff frequency is a genuine codec brickwall
 * filter (e.g., 128/192 kbps MP3) vs. natural vocal or SFX roll-off.
 */
export function detectCodecBrickwall(
  e98Db: Float32Array,
  sampleRate: number,
  fftSize: number
): { isTranscoded: boolean; cutoffHz: number; slopeDbPerOctave: number } {
  const binHz = sampleRate / fftSize;
  const nyquist = sampleRate / 2;

  // Lossy codecs place low-pass filters between 14.5 kHz and 20.5 kHz
  const minCodecBin = Math.floor(14500 / binHz);
  const maxCodecBin = Math.min(e98Db.length - 4, Math.ceil(20500 / binHz));

  let steepestDrop = 0;
  let detectedCutoffHz = nyquist;

  for (let b = minCodecBin; b <= maxCodecBin; b++) {
    const fLow = b * binHz;
    // Measure energy drop across a narrow 1.15x frequency transition band (~0.2 octaves)
    const bHigh = Math.min(e98Db.length - 1, Math.round((fLow * 1.15) / binHz));
    if (bHigh <= b) continue;

    // Compare local passband average vs. stopband average above the cliff
    const passbandDb = (e98Db[b - 2] + e98Db[b - 1] + e98Db[b]) / 3;
    const stopbandDb = (e98Db[bHigh] + e98Db[Math.min(e98Db.length - 1, bHigh + 1)]) / 2;

    const dropDb = passbandDb - stopbandDb;
    const octaves = Math.log2((bHigh * binHz) / fLow);
    const slope = octaves > 0 ? dropDb / octaves : 0;

    // Require a genuine cliff (>= 60 dB/octave) dropping into the noise floor (< -78 dBFS)
    if (dropDb >= 18 && slope >= 60 && stopbandDb < -78 && slope > steepestDrop) {
      steepestDrop = slope;
      detectedCutoffHz = fLow;
    }
  }

  return {
    isTranscoded: steepestDrop >= 60,
    cutoffHz: Math.round(detectedCutoffHz),
    slopeDbPerOctave: Math.round(steepestDrop * 10) / 10,
  };
}

With this dual gate, a clean 48 kHz voice line or bass-heavy explosion SFX with natural roll-off (18–25 dB/octave) is never falsely accused of being a 128 kbps MP3, while actual lossy transcodes are caught within ±300 Hz.

3. Fix #2: Mel-Scale Spectrograms & Sub-Sample YIN Pitch ($F_0$)

When inspecting dialogue or tonal game SFX on a standard linear spectrogram (0 Hz – 24,000 Hz), the entire human vocal range (80 Hz – 3,500 Hz) is squashed into the bottom 14% of the canvas—leaving the top 86% nearly blank.

Mapping the vertical canvas axis to the perceptual Mel scale expands the 50 Hz – 8 kHz vocal and SFX band across 75% of the viewport:

$$m(f) = 2595 cdot log_{10}left(1 + rac{f}{700}
ight), quad f(m) = 700 cdot left(10^{m / 2595} - 1
ight)$$

And for voice actors checking pitch consistency or sound designers tuning tonal assets, FFT bin resolution at low frequencies is too coarse (48000 / 2048 = 23.4 Hz per bin—wider than a musical semitone at C3!). Instead, use time-domain YIN Cumulative Mean Normalized Difference ($d'( au)$) with parabolic interpolation for sub-Hz $F_0$ accuracy:

export function estimateYinPitchHz(frame: Float32Array, sampleRate: number): number | null {
  const halfLen = frame.length >> 1;
  const minTau = Math.floor(sampleRate / 1000); // Max 1000 Hz
  const maxTau = Math.min(halfLen - 1, Math.ceil(sampleRate / 55)); // Min 55 Hz (A1)

  const diff = new Float32Array(maxTau + 1);
  const cmnd = new Float32Array(maxTau + 1);
  cmnd[0] = 1;

  let runningSum = 0;
  for (let tau = 1; tau <= maxTau; tau++) {
    let sum = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < halfLen; i++) {
      const delta = frame[i] - frame[i + tau];
      sum += delta * delta;
    }
    diff[tau] = sum;
    runningSum += sum;
    cmnd[tau] = runningSum > 0 ? (diff[tau] * tau) / runningSum : 1;
  }

  // Find first dip below threshold (0.15)
  let bestTau = -1;
  for (let tau = minTau; tau <= maxTau; tau++) {
    if (cmnd[tau] < 0.15) {
      while (tau + 1 <= maxTau && cmnd[tau + 1] < cmnd[tau]) tau++;
      bestTau = tau;
      break;
    }
  }
  if (bestTau === -1) return null;

  // Parabolic interpolation for sub-sample precision
  const y1 = cmnd[Math.max(1, bestTau - 1)];
  const y2 = cmnd[bestTau];
  const y3 = cmnd[Math.min(maxTau, bestTau + 1)];
  const denom = y1 - 2 * y2 + y3;
  const refinedTau = denom !== 0 ? bestTau + (y1 - y3) / (2 * denom) : bestTau;

  return sampleRate / refinedTau;
}

4. Fix #3: Click-Free Game Audio Loops (Zero-Crossing + Equal-Power Crossfade)

Another classic game dev headache: you trim an ambient wind or engine loop, set audioSource.loop = true in Unity, Unreal, or Godot, and hear a sharp pop/click every time the buffer wraps from the end back to sample 0.

Two things cause this:

  1. Non-Zero Boundary Discontinuity: The last sample ends at +0.42 while sample 0 starts at -0.18, creating an instantaneous step function (infinite high-frequency transient).
  2. Linear Crossfade Dip: If you overlap the tail and head using a linear fade (1 - t and t), uncorrelated ambient signals suffer a -3 dB volume dip in the middle of the crossfade because $(0.5)^2 + (0.5)^2 = 0.5$ power.

Instead, snap trim handles to rising zero-crossings and apply an Equal-Power ($cos / sin$) Crossfade where $cos^2( heta) + sin^2( heta) = 1.0$:

export function applyEqualPowerLoopCrossfade(
  samples: Float32Array,
  crossfadeSamples: number
): Float32Array {
  const outLen = samples.length - crossfadeSamples;
  const out = new Float32Array(outLen);

  // Copy main body after the crossfade region
  out.set(samples.subarray(crossfadeSamples, outLen), crossfadeSamples);

  // Blend the tail into the head using constant-power trig gains
  for (let i = 0; i < crossfadeSamples; i++) {
    const t = i / crossfadeSamples; // 0 -> 1
    const angle = t * (Math.PI * 0.5);
    const gainIn = Math.sin(angle);  // Head fades in (0 -> 1)
    const gainOut = Math.cos(angle); // Tail fades out (1 -> 0)

    const headSample = samples[i];
    const tailSample = samples[outLen + i];
    out[i] = headSample * gainIn + tailSample * gainOut;
  }

  return out;
}

  2. 👉 Game Audio Seamless Looper & Normalizer (/audio-looper) Interactive canvas drag-trimming, automatic zero-crossing snap, equal-power ($cos/sin$) seamless loop crossfading, LUFS normalization, and multi-bit WAV export.
  3. 👉 Frequency Tone & Game SFX Synthesizer (/tone-generator) 4-stage ADSR envelope + logarithmic frequency sweep synthesizer for speaker calibration and retro game sound effects.
